arXiv:2303.12592v4 [math.RT] 14 Feb 2024

BPS algebras and generalised Kac–Moody algebras from 2-Calabi–Yau categories

Ben Davison , Lucien Hennecart and Sebastian Schlegel Mejia Address: School of Mathematics, University of Edinburgh, Edinburgh, UK Email address: Ben.Davison@ed.ac.uk Email address: Lucien.Hennecart@ed.ac.uk Address: Max Planck Institute for Mathematics, Vivatsgasse 7, 53111 Bonn, Germany Email address: schlegel@mpim-bonn.mpg.de
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We determine the structure of the BPS algebra of 22-Calabi–Yau Abelian categories whose stack of objects admits a good moduli space. We prove that this algebra is isomorphic to the positive part of the enveloping algebra of a generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra generated by the intersection cohomology of certain connected components (corresponding to roots) of the good moduli space. Some major examples include the BPS algebras of (1) the category of semistable coherent sheaves of given slope on a K3 surface or, more generally, quasiprojective symplectic surface, (2) semistable Higgs bundles on smooth projective curves, (3) preprojective algebras of quivers, (4) multiplicative preprojective algebras and (5) fundamental groups of (quiver) Riemann surfaces. We define the BPS Lie algebras of 22-Calabi–Yau categories and prove that they coincide with the ones obtained by dimensional reduction from the critical cohomological Hall algebra in the case in which the 2-Calabi–Yau category is the category of representations of a preprojective algebra. Consequences include (1) A proof in full generality of the Bozec–Schiffmann positivity conjecture for absolutely cuspidal polynomials, a strengthening of the Kac positivity conjecture (2) A proof of the cohomological integrality conjecture for the category of semistable coherent sheaves on local K3 surfaces (3) A description of the cohomology (in all degrees) of Nakajima quiver varieties as direct sums of irreducible lowest weight representations over the BPS Lie algebra.

1. Introduction

In this paper, we study connections between generalised Kac–Moody (also known as Borcherds) Lie algebras, and the Borel–Moore homology of stacks of objects of 22-Calabi–Yau (2CY) Abelian categories. 2CY categories feature prominently in geometric representation theory, mathematical physics, algebraic geometry and nonabelian Hodge theory. Concrete examples of such categories include representations of various flavours of preprojective algebras, categories of coherent sheaves on K3 surfaces, and categories of Higgs bundles. We prove our results via the BPS algebras defined in [DHS22], following the sequence of papers [HM96, KS11, DM20].

In the original paper [HM96] on BPS algebras of Harvey and Moore, a physical argument for the appearance of generalised Kac–Moody algebras in algebras of BPS states is given. In the study of operators via correspondences on Hilbert schemes of points on 𝐀2\mathbf{A}^{2}, it was shown by Nakajima and Grojnowski [Nak97, Gro96] that an infinite-dimensional Heisenberg algebra, which is a very particular generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra, plays a central role. These papers in turn were inspired by the pioneering work of Nakajima [Nak94], in which the deep connection between (usual) Kac–Moody Lie algebras and algebras of correspondences on quiver varieties was first uncovered. In this paper we explain how every suitably geometric 2CY category gives rise to a (generalised) Kac–Moody Lie algebra. More precisely, we show that the BPS algebra of a 2CY category 𝒜\mathcal{A} with good moduli stack of objects is the universal enveloping algebra of one half of a generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra, and that the Cartan datum of this Lie algebra is explicitly given in terms of intersection cohomology of certain coarse moduli spaces of objects in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Special cases of (the doubled versions of) these BPS Lie algebras are identified with algebras of correspondences appearing in [Nak94, Nak97, Nak98, Gro96]; indeed part of our motivation was to find a unified explanation for all of these results. On the other hand, our results apply to very general 2CY categories. Reflecting the range of 2CY categories in mathematics, we can then use our structural results to prove conjectures in combinatorics, representation theory, and algebraic geometry.

For the combinatorial applications, we consider certain functions counting isomorphism classes of representations of quivers over finite fields. A consequence of the main theorem applied to the category Rep⁡ΠQ\operatorname{Rep}\Pi_{Q} of representations of the preprojective algebra of a quiver is a proof in full generality of the Bozec–Schiffmann positivity conjecture for (absolutely) cuspidal polynomials of quivers [BS19]. This is a strengthening of the positivity of Kac polynomials conjectured in [Kac83]. As in the proofs [HLR13, Dav18, DGT16] of the Kac positivity conjecture, we prove the positivity of absolutely cuspidal polynomials by identifying their coefficients with dimensions of certain vector spaces, more specifically by identifying these polynomials with intersection Poincaré polynomials of singular Nakajima varieties. We also define and prove the positivity of nilpotent and 11-nilpotent absolutely cuspidal polynomials, which are associated to nilpotent and 11-nilpotent Kac polynomials counting representations of quivers over finite fields satisfying various nilpotency conditions [BSV20].

In geometric representation theory, we apply our main result also to understanding the cohomology of Nakajima quiver varieties as representations over the BPS Lie algebra. Applying the main theorem to the category of Rep⁡ΠQ𝐟\operatorname{Rep}\Pi_{Q_{\mathbf{f}}}-modules, where Q𝐟Q_{\mathbf{f}} is a framed quiver, we describe a decomposition of the entire cohomology of Nakajima quiver varieties (i.e. in all cohomological degrees) into irreducible lowest weight modules for the (doubled) BPS Lie algebra. Since this Lie algebra contains the usual Kac–Moody Lie algebra associated to the unframed quiver QQ, this answers a longstanding question of Nakajima regarding the possibility of extending his famous decomposition of (part of) the cohomology of quiver varieties into irreducible lowest weight modules. This provides a unified framework for constructing the action of Kac–Moody Lie algebras and Heisenberg algebras on cohomology of various quiver varieties [Nak97, Nak98], as well as cohomology of more general moduli spaces of objects in 2CY categories.

Within enumerative algebraic geometry, and more specifically cohomological Donaldson–Thomas theory [DM20, Sze14], we use our results to prove the cohomological integrality theorem for general 2CY categories and their undeformed 3CY completions. The 2CY version of this conjecture states that there is an isomorphism

HBM⁡(𝔐𝒜,𝐐¯vir)≅Sym⁡(⨁a∈K⁡(𝒜)ℱ¯a⊗H⁡(B⁡𝐂∗,𝐐))\HO^{\BoMo}(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}},\underline{\mathbf{Q}}^{\mathrm{vir}})\cong\Sym\left(\bigoplus_{a\in\K(\mathcal{A})}\underline{\mathcal{F}}_{a}\otimes\HO(\B\mathbf{C}^{*},\mathbf{Q})\right)

where 𝔐𝒜\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}} is the stack of objects in a fixed 2CY category 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Up to a cohomological shift the left hand side is the Borel–Moore homology of 𝔐𝒜\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}, and each ℱ¯a\underline{\mathcal{F}}_{a} is a bounded complex of mixed Hodge structures. We prove this by proving a stronger relative version, in terms of the tensor category of mixed Hodge modules on the coarse moduli space ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}. The above isomorphism is reminiscent of a PBW-type isomorphism, and indeed we prove it by producing a (relative) PBW isomorphism for the CoHA associated to 𝒜\mathcal{A}. Via dimensional reduction [Kin22], the theorem implies the cohomological integrality conjecture regarding the 3CY completion of 2CY categories; a concrete consequence is the (refined) integrality theorem for the DT partition function of local K3 surfaces. In the rest of the introduction we explain, connect and motivate these results in more depth.

1.1. Generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebras

Our main structural theorems in §1.2 are expressed in terms of generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebras, and their positive halves, which we briefly introduce in this section.

1.1.1. Generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebras associated to a monoid with bilinear form and weight function

Let (M,+)(M,+) be a monoid. Often, we will take MM such that the natural map M→M^M\rightarrow\widehat{M} to the groupification is an inclusion into a lattice (which becomes convenient when considering Weyl group actions). Let (−,−):M×M→𝐙(-,-)\colon M\times M\rightarrow\mathbf{Z} be a symmetric bilinear form. In §3.1, we define the sets of primitive positive roots ΣM,(−,−)\Sigma_{M,(-,-)}, simple positive roots ΦM,(−,−)+\Phi^{+}_{M,(-,-)} and the Cartan matrix AM,(−,−)=(am,n=(m,n))m,n∈ΦM,(−,−)+A_{M,(-,-)}=(a_{m,n}=(m,n))_{m,n\in\Phi^{+}_{M,(-,-)}}. We assume that am,m∈2​𝐙⩽1a_{m,m}\in 2\mathbf{Z}_{\leqslant 1} and that am,n⩽0a_{m,n}\leqslant 0 if am,m=2a_{m,m}=2. For a function

P:ΦM,(−,−)+→𝐍[t±1/2]m↦Pm​(t)\begin{matrix}P&\colon&\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}&\rightarrow&\mathbf{N}[t^{\pm 1/2}]\\ &&m&\mapsto&P_{m}(t)\end{matrix}

such that Pm​(t)=1P_{m}(t)=1 if am,m=2a_{m,m}=2, we define a M^×𝐙\widehat{M}\times\mathbf{Z}-graded generalised Kac–Moody algebra 𝔤M,(−,−),P\mathfrak{g}_{M,(-,-),P} (in the sense of Borcherds [Bor88], see [BS19] for the graded version) associated to this datum, by generators and relations. We refer to such a function as a weight function. The Lie algebra 𝔤M,(−,−),P\mathfrak{g}_{M,(-,-),P} has a triangular decomposition 𝔤M,(−,−),P=𝔫M,(−,−),P−⊕𝔥M,(−,−)⊕𝔫M,(−,−),P+\mathfrak{g}_{M,(-,-),P}=\mathfrak{n}^{-}_{M,(-,-),P}\oplus\mathfrak{h}_{M,(-,-)}\oplus\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{M,(-,-),P}. We also have a description by generators and relations (see §3.2) and a triangular decomposition of its enveloping algebra

𝐔⁡(𝔤M,(−,−),P)≅𝐔⁡(𝔫M,(−,−),P−)⊗𝐔⁡(𝔥M,(−,−))⊗𝐔⁡(𝔫M,(−,−),P+).\UEA(\mathfrak{g}_{M,(-,-),P})\cong\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{-}_{M,(-,-),P})\otimes\UEA(\mathfrak{h}_{M,(-,-)})\otimes\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{M,(-,-),P}).

Both 𝔫M,(−,−),P+\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{M,(-,-),P} and 𝐔⁡(𝔫M,(−,−),P+)\UEA(\mathfrak{n}_{M,(-,-),P}^{+}) are M×𝐙M\times\mathbf{Z}-graded.

In concrete situations, the polynomial Pm​(t)P_{m}(t) is the graded dimension of some given vector space VmV_{m}. The above algebra is the unique (up to isomorphism, and some choice regarding the Cartan subalgebra) cohomologically graded generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra with generators in the mmth root weight space identified with VmV_{m}.

1.1.2. Positive halves of generalised Kac–Moody (Lie) algebras in symmetric tensor categories of perverse sheaves or mixed Hodge modules

Let (ℳ,⊕)(\mathcal{M},\oplus) be a commutative monoid in the category of complex schemes, for which we have a decomposition ℳ=∐m∈Mℳm\mathcal{M}=\coprod_{m\in M}\mathcal{M}_{m} into finite type unions of finite type connected components ℳm\mathcal{M}_{m} of ℳ\mathcal{M} (i.e. ℳm\mathcal{M}_{m} might be disconnected but it is a finite type scheme) for some monoid (M,+)(M,+) as in §1.1.1. We assume that this decomposition is respected by ⊕\oplus (we allow ℳ\mathcal{M} to have infinitely many connected components). In this case, we do not have a groupification ℳ^\widehat{\mathcal{M}} with which to define the full generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra with generators for positive roots given by some selection of sheaves on ℳ\mathcal{M}, but we nonetheless can define the positive half of such a Lie algebra.

We let (−,−):M×M→𝐙(-,-)\colon M\times M\rightarrow\mathbf{Z} be a bilinear form, ΣM,(−,−)\Sigma_{M,(-,-)} be the set of primitive positive roots, ΦM,(−,−)+\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+} be the set of simple positive roots and AM,(−,−)A_{M,(-,-)} be the Cartan matrix as in §1.1.1. We assume that ℳm=pt\mathcal{M}_{m}=\mathrm{pt} for any m∈ΦM,(−,−)+,m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\real} and that the sum map +:M×M→M+\colon M\times M\rightarrow M is finite.

Let 𝒢¯m∈MHM⁡(ℳm)\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{m}\in\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{m}) be a set of mixed Hodge modules indexed by m∈ΦM,(−,−)+m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}. We assume that 𝒢¯m=𝐐¯ℳm=𝐐¯pt\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{m}=\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathcal{M}_{m}}=\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathrm{pt}} is the constant mixed Hodge module if m∈ΦM,(−,−)+,m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\real}. We let PP be the weight function given by the Poincaré polynomials of these 𝒢¯m\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{m}:

P:ΦM,(−,−)+→𝐍[t±1/2]m↦P⁡(𝒢¯m)=∑j∈𝐙dimHj⁡(𝒢¯m)​tj/2.\begin{matrix}P\colon&\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}&\rightarrow&\mathbf{N}[t^{\pm 1/2}]&\\ &m&\mapsto&P(\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{m})&=\sum_{j\in\mathbf{Z}}\dim\HO^{j}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{m})t^{j/2}.\end{matrix}

We define 𝔫ℳ,𝒢¯+\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},\underline{\mathscr{G}}} to be the free Lie algebra object generated by 𝒢¯=⨁m∈M𝒢¯m\underline{\mathscr{G}}=\bigoplus_{m\in M}\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{m} in the symmetric tensor category MHM⁡(ℳ)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}), quotiented by the Lie ideal generated by generalised Serre relations (see §3.2 for the precise construction). The Lie algebra obtained by taking derived global sections of 𝔫ℳ,𝒢¯+\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},\underline{\mathscr{G}}} and forgetting the mixed Hodge structures is isomorphic to 𝔫M,(−,−),P+\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{M,(-,-),P}, (half) the generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra defined as in §1.1.1.

Similarly we define 𝐔⁡(𝔫ℳ,𝒢¯+)\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},\underline{\mathscr{G}}}) to be the free unital associative algebra generated by 𝒢¯\underline{\mathscr{G}}, quotiented by the two-sided ideal generated by the same relations. The algebra obtained by taking derived global sections and forgetting the MHS of 𝐔⁡(𝔫ℳ,𝒢¯+)\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},\underline{\mathscr{G}}}) is isomorphic to 𝐔⁡(𝔫M,(−,−),P+)\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{M,(-,-),P}).

1.2. The BPS algebra of a 2-Calabi–Yau category

We let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an Abelian 2-Calabi–Yau category in the sense of [DHS22]. It is an Abelian subcategory of the homotopy category of some ambient dg category 𝒞\mathscr{C}. We briefly recall in §4 the assumptions on 𝒜\mathcal{A}. In particular, we assume that it has a moduli stack of objects, 𝔐𝒜\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}} which is an Artin stack with a good moduli space 𝙹𝙷𝒜:𝔐𝒜→ℳ𝒜\JH_{\mathcal{A}}\colon\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} (as defined in [Alp13]). The good moduli space ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} is assumed to be a scheme and it has the monoid structure ⊕:ℳ𝒜×ℳ𝒜→ℳ𝒜\oplus\colon\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\to\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} induced by the direct sum ⊕:𝔐𝒜×𝔐𝒜→𝔐𝒜\oplus\colon\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}. The complex of mixed Hodge modules 𝒜¯𝒜≔(𝙹𝙷𝒜)∗​𝔻​𝐐¯𝔐𝒜vir∈𝒟+​(MHM⁡(ℳ𝒜))\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\coloneqq(\JH_{\mathcal{A}})_{*}\mathbb{D}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}}^{\mathrm{vir}}\in\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}})) is the relative cohomological Hall algebra, where the multiplication

𝔪:𝒜¯𝒜⊡𝒜¯𝒜→𝒜¯𝒜\mathfrak{m}\colon\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\boxdot\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}

has been defined in [DHS22]. The superscript vir\mathrm{vir} indicates a twist by a certain power of the Tate twist which we make precise in §6.1. The complex of mixed Hodge modules 𝒜¯𝒜\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}} is concentrated in nonnegative cohomological degrees and the degree 00 cohomology, ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg≔ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}\coloneqq\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}), carries the induced multiplication ℋ0​(𝔪)\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathfrak{m}). It is called the BPS algebra sheaf.

We let (−,−)𝒞(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}} be the Euler form of the category 𝒞\mathscr{C}. It induces a symmetric bilinear form

(−,−)𝒞:π0​(ℳ𝒜)×π0​(ℳ𝒜)→𝐙(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}}\colon\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}})\times\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}})\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}

such that (a,a)𝒞≡0(mod2)(a,a)_{\mathscr{C}}\equiv 0\pmod{2} for any a∈π0​(ℳ𝒜)a\in\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}). We fix a monoid K⁡(𝒜)\K(\mathcal{A}), which we assume is a submonoid of a lattice, and a surjective morphism with finite fibres cl:π0​(ℳ𝒜)→K⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{cl}\colon\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}})\rightarrow\K(\mathcal{A}) such that the Euler form factors through cl\mathrm{cl}. We choose a bilinear form ψ\psi on K⁡(𝒜)\K(\mathcal{A}) such that for any a,b∈K⁡(𝒜)a,b\in\K(\mathcal{A}), we have ψ⁡(a,b)+ψ⁡(b,a)≡(a,b)𝒞(mod2)\psi(a,b)+\psi(b,a)\equiv(a,b)_{\mathscr{C}}\pmod{2}. We twist the CoHA multiplication 𝔪\mathfrak{m} by ψ\psi: 𝔪a,bψ≔(−1)ψ⁡(a,b)​𝔪a,b\mathfrak{m}_{a,b}^{\psi}\coloneqq(-1)^{\psi(a,b)}\mathfrak{m}_{a,b} for a,b∈K⁡(𝒜)a,b\in\K(\mathcal{A}), where 𝔪a,b\mathfrak{m}_{a,b} is the restriction of 𝔪\mathfrak{m} to ℳ𝒜,a×ℳ𝒜,b\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},a}\times\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},b}, and ℳ𝒜,a\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},a} denotes the union of connected components corresponding to cl−1​(a)\mathrm{cl}^{-1}(a). This defines the ψ\psi-twisted multiplication 𝔪ψ\mathfrak{m}^{\psi} on the relative algebras 𝒜¯𝒜\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}, ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}} and the absolute algebras H∗⁡𝒜¯𝒜\HO^{*}\!\!\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}, BPS¯𝒜,Alg\underline{\mathrm{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}. We denote by 𝒜¯𝒜ψ\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi}, ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Algψ\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}, H∗⁡𝒜¯𝒜ψ\HO^{*}\!\!\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi} and BPS¯𝒜,Algψ\underline{\mathrm{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi} the algebras with their twisted multiplications.

We let ΣK⁡(𝒜)≔ΣK⁡(𝒜),(−,−)𝒞\Sigma_{\K(\mathcal{A})}\coloneqq\Sigma_{\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}}} and ΦK⁡(𝒜)+≔ΦK⁡(𝒜),(−,−)𝒞+\Phi^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A})}\coloneqq\Phi^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}}} be the sets of primitive positive roots and simple positive roots respectively (for the monoid with bilinear form (K⁡(𝒜),(−,−)𝒞)(\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}})), as in §3.1. For m∈ΦK⁡(𝒜)+,isom\in\Phi_{\K(\mathcal{A})}^{+,\mathrm{iso}}, we write m=l​m′m=lm^{\prime} for m′∈ΣK⁡(𝒜)m^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{\K(\mathcal{A})} and l∈𝐍l\in\mathbf{N}. This decomposition of mm is unique and we have a natural closed immersion

um:ℳ𝒜,m′→ℳ𝒜,mx↦x⊕l.\begin{matrix}u_{m}&\colon&\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m^{\prime}}&\rightarrow&\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m}\\ &&x&\mapsto&x^{\oplus l}.\end{matrix}

The (connected components of the) complex scheme ℳ𝒜,m′\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m^{\prime}} are of dimension 22 (Proposition 5.4) and we let 𝒢′¯m=(um)∗​(ℐ​𝒞¯​(ℳ𝒜,m′))\underline{\mathscr{G}^{\prime}}_{m}=(u_{m})_{*}(\underline{\mathcal{IC}}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m^{\prime}})). Then for m∈ΦK⁡(𝒜)+m\in\Phi^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A})} we define

𝒢¯m≔{ℐ​𝒞¯​(ℳ𝒜,m)if ​m∈ΦK⁡(𝒜)+∖ΦK⁡(𝒜)+,iso(um)∗​(ℐ​𝒞¯​(ℳ𝒜,m′))if m=lm′∈ΦK⁡(𝒜)+,iso,m′∈ΣK⁡(𝒜).\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{m}\coloneqq\begin{cases}\underline{\mathcal{IC}}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m})&\textrm{if }m\in\Phi^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A})}\smallsetminus\Phi_{\K(\mathcal{A})}^{+,\mathrm{iso}}\\ (u_{m})_{*}(\underline{\mathcal{IC}}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m^{\prime}}))&\textrm{if }m=lm^{\prime}\in\Phi_{\K(\mathcal{A})}^{+,\mathrm{iso}},\;m^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{\K(\mathcal{A})}.\end{cases}

Its restriction to each of the connected components of ℳ𝒜,m\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m} is simple.

1.2.1. BPS algebras as GKM algebras

We let 𝒢¯=⨁m∈ΦK⁡(𝒜)+𝒢¯m\underline{\mathscr{G}}=\bigoplus_{m\in\Phi_{\K(\mathcal{A})}^{+}}\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{m} be as defined above. Note that 𝒢¯m≅𝐐¯pt\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{m}\cong\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathrm{pt}} if m∈ΦK⁡(𝒜)+,m\in\Phi_{\K(\mathcal{A})}^{+,\real}. We can finally state our first main theorem, proved in §7.7.

Theorem 1.1.

There exists a canonical isomorphism of algebra objects

𝐔⁡(𝔫ℳ𝒜,(−,−)𝒞,𝒢¯+)→≅ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Algψ\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}},(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}},\underline{\mathscr{G}}})\xrightarrow{\cong}\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}

in MHM⁡(ℳ𝒜)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}).

Recall that BPS¯𝒜,Algψ≔H∗⁡(ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Algψ)\underline{\mathrm{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}\coloneqq\HO^{*}(\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}) is the algebra formed by taking the derived global sections of the BPS algebra sheaf. It is an ordinary K⁡(𝒜)×𝐙\K(\mathcal{A})\times\mathbf{Z}-graded algebra (where the copy of 𝐙\mathbf{Z} encodes the cohomological grading) and it is called the BPS algebra. By construction, it has a lift to an algebra object in the category of mixed Hodge structures.

If ı△:ℳ𝒜△↪ℳ𝒜\imath_{\triangle}\colon\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} is a locally closed inclusion of a saturated submonoid, the complex ı!△ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Algψ\imath^{!}_{\triangle}\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi} inherits the structure of an algebra object in the derived category of mixed Hodge modules on ℳ𝒜△\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle} via restriction, and we similarly define the △\triangle BPS algebra by taking derived global sections:

BPS¯𝒜,Alg△,ψ≔H∗(ℳ𝒜△,ı△!ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Algψ).\underline{\mathrm{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\triangle,\psi}\coloneqq\HO^{*}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle},\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}).

Applying the functor ı△!\imath_{\triangle}^{!} and taking derived global sections in Theorem 1.1 implies our main result on BPS algebras:

Theorem 1.2.

There is a canonical isomorphism of algebras

𝐔(𝔫K(𝒜),(−,−)𝒞,H∗(ı△!𝒢)+)→≅BPS𝒜,Alg△,ψ.\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}},\HO^{*}(\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\mathscr{G})})\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathrm{BPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\triangle,\psi}.

and thus an isomorphism of algebras

𝐔⁡(𝔫K⁡(𝒜),(−,−)𝒞,IP𝒜△+)→≅BPS𝒜,Alg△,ψ,\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}},\mathrm{IP}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}}})\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathrm{BPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\triangle,\psi},

where IP𝒜△\mathrm{IP}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}} is the weight function

In particular, there is an embedding

BPS𝒜,Alg△,ψ⊆𝐔⁡(𝔤K⁡(𝒜),(−,−)𝒞,IP𝒜△)\mathrm{BPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\triangle,\psi}\subseteq\UEA(\mathfrak{g}_{\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}},\mathrm{IP}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}}})

of the BPS algebra as the positive half of a cohomologically graded generalised Kac–Moody algebra.

Explicitly, for m∈ΣK⁡(𝒜)⊆ΦK⁡(𝒜)+m\in\Sigma_{\K(\mathcal{A})}\subseteq\Phi_{\K(\mathcal{A})}^{+}, IP𝒜△​(m)\mathrm{IP}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}}(m) is the Poincaré polynomial of H∗(ℳ𝒜,m△,ı△!ℐ𝒞(ℳ𝒜,m))\HO^{*}\!(\mathcal{M}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A},m},\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\mathcal{IC}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m})), and for m=l​m′m=lm^{\prime} with m′∈Σ𝒜m^{\prime}\in\Sigma_{\mathcal{A}} isotropic, IP𝒜△​(m)\mathrm{IP}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}}(m) is the Poincaré polynomial of H∗(ℳ𝒜,m′△,ı△!ℐ𝒞(ℳ𝒜,m′))\HO^{*}\!(\mathcal{M}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A},m^{\prime}},\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\mathcal{IC}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m^{\prime}})), so that spaces of simple roots of 𝔤𝒜BPS,△\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle} defined below are identified with ı△\imath_{\triangle}-restrictions of intersection complexes on moduli spaces of objects of 𝒜\mathcal{A}.

We let 𝒜\mathcal{A}, 𝔐𝒜\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}, ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} be as in §1.2. Motivated by Theorem 1.1, we define the relative BPS Lie algebra of 𝒜\mathcal{A} as

(1.1) ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie≔𝔫ℳ𝒜,(−,−)𝒞,𝒢¯+,\displaystyle\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}\coloneqq\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}},(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}},\underline{\mathscr{G}}},

we define

(1.2) 𝔫¯𝒜BPS,△,+≔H∗(ℳ𝒜△,ı△!ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie)\underline{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle,+}_{\mathcal{A}}\coloneqq\HO^{*}(\mathcal{M}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}},\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}})

so that

(1.3) 𝔫𝒜BPS,△,+≔\displaystyle\mathfrak{n}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle,+}_{\mathcal{A}}\coloneqq H∗(ℳ𝒜△,ı△!ℬ𝒫𝒮𝒜,Lie)\displaystyle\HO^{*}(\mathcal{M}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}},\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\mathcal{BPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}})
≅\displaystyle\cong 𝔫+K(𝒜),(−,−)𝒞,H∗(ℳ△𝒜,ı△!𝒢)\displaystyle\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}},\HO^{*}(\mathcal{M}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}},\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\mathscr{G})}

and define the full BPS Lie algebra:

By construction, the full BPS Lie algebra is a generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra containing the BPS Lie algebra H∗(ℳ𝒜△,ı△!ℬ𝒫𝒮𝒜,Lie)\HO^{*}(\mathcal{M}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}},\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\mathcal{BPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}) as its strictly positive half.

1.3. Positivity for cuspidal polynomials

Cuspidal polynomials CQ,𝐝​(q)C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q) of a quiver QQ were introduced in [BS19], and defined as the polynomials counting the dimensions of the graded components of the space of primitive elements of the constructible Hall algebra HQ,𝐅qH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}} over a finite field. The primitive elements are defined using Green’s coproduct on HQ,𝐅qH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}} [Gre95] and they form a minimal subspace generating the Hall algebra [SV01]. See [Sch18] for motivation and background for this subsection.

Bozec and Schiffmann also defined a closely related family of polynomials, the absolutely cuspidal polynomials CQ,𝐝abs​(q)C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{abs}}(q). They are defined in a combinatorial way from cuspidal polynomials and coincide with the latter for hyperbolic dimension vectors. More precisely, CQ,𝐝​(q)=CQ,𝐝abs​(q)C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)=C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{abs}}(q) if (𝐝,𝐝)Q<0(\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d})_{Q}<0, CQ,𝐝​(q)=CQ,𝐝abs​(q)=qgiC_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)=C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{abs}}(q)=q^{g_{i}} if 𝐝=1i∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}=1_{i}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} is a basis vector and the vertex ii carries gig_{i} loops, and, if (𝐝,𝐝)Q=0(\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d})_{Q}=0 with 𝐝\mathbf{d} indivisible, then the families (CQ,l​𝐝​(q))l⩾1(C_{Q,l\mathbf{d}}(q))_{l\geqslant 1} and (CQ,l​𝐝abs​(q))l⩾1(C_{Q,l\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{abs}}(q))_{l\geqslant 1} are related by the formula utilising plethystic exponentials (see for example [BS19, §1.5] for a definition of this combinatorial operation)

Expz⁡(∑l⩾1CQ,l​𝐝​(q)​zl​𝐝)=Expz,q⁡(∑l⩾1CQ,l​𝐝abs​(q)​zl​𝐝).\Exp_{z}\left(\sum_{l\geqslant 1}C_{Q,l\mathbf{d}}(q)z^{l\mathbf{d}}\right)=\Exp_{z,q}\left(\sum_{l\geqslant 1}C_{Q,l\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{abs}}(q)z^{l\mathbf{d}}\right).

Bozec and Schiffmann formulated the following positivity conjecture for the family (CQ,𝐝abs​(q))𝐝∈𝐍Q0(C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{abs}}(q))_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}}:

Conjecture 1.3 ([BS19]).

For 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}, the polynomial CQ,𝐝abs​(q)C^{\mathrm{abs}}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q) has nonnegative coefficients.

By taking the Serre subcategories of the category Rep⁡(Q)\operatorname{Rep}(Q) of finite dimensional representations of QQ, of nilpotent representations, Repnil⁡(Q)\operatorname{Rep}^{\mathrm{nil}}(Q), and of 11-nilpotent representations, Rep1​-nil⁡(Q)\operatorname{Rep}^{1\snil}(Q) (§9.3.1), one can consider the associated constructible Hall algebras HQ,𝐅qnilH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{nil}} and HQ,𝐅q1​-nilH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{1\snil}. We have inclusions of bialgebras HQ,𝐅Qnil⊆HQ,𝐅q1​-nil⊆HQ,𝐅qH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{Q}}^{\mathrm{nil}}\subseteq H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{1\snil}\subseteq H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}. As in [BS19], we define the nilpotent cuspidal polynomials CQ,𝐝nil​(q)C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{nil}}(q) and 11-nilpotent cuspidal polynomials CQ,𝐝1​-nil​(q)C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{1\snil}(q) as the dimension counts of primitive elements of the twisted bialgebras HQ,𝐅qnilH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{nil}} and HQ,𝐅1​-nilH_{Q,\mathbf{F}}^{1\snil} respectively, as well as their absolute versions CQ,𝐝nil,abs​(q)C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{nil},\mathrm{abs}}(q) and CQ,𝐝1​-nil,abs​(q)C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{1\snil,\mathrm{abs}}(q). We may therefore formulate in the same way the positivity conjecture for these new families of polynomials.

We prove all these conjectures in this paper.

Theorem 1.4 (Theorems 9.5 and 9.12).

Absolutely cuspidal polynomials have nonnegative coefficients (Conjecture 1.3 is true). Additionally, absolutely cuspidal nilpotent and 11-nilpotent polynomials have nonnegative coefficients.

A key fact in the proof of the positivity conjectures is the interpretation of cuspidal polynomials as graded multiplicities of simple roots. Namely, for the monoid M=𝐍Q0M=\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} with the symmetrised Euler form and a weight function PP as in §1.1.1, there is a combinatorial formula giving the character of the positive part of the GKM Lie algebra 𝔤M,(−,−),P\mathfrak{g}_{M,(-,-),P} (a generalization of the Weyl character formula). In the graded context, it is described in details in [BS19]. By letting PP vary, we obtain a function

WQ:{P:ΦM,(−,−)+→𝐍[q±1/2]}→𝐍[q±1/2][[M]].W_{Q}:\{P\colon\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbf{N}[q^{\pm 1/2}]\}\rightarrow\mathbf{N}[q^{\pm 1/2}][\![M]\!].

sending a weight function to the character of the corresponding positive part of the generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra.

Proposition 1.5 ([BS19]).

The map WQW_{Q} is injective and if Expz,t⁡(∑𝐝∈𝐍Q0AQ,𝐝​(t)​z𝐝)\Exp_{z,t}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}}A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(t)z^{\mathbf{d}}\right) is in its image, then it is the image under WQW_{Q} of the weight function 𝐝↦CQ,𝐝abs​(t)\mathbf{d}\mapsto C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{abs}}(t) (we denote by AQ,𝐝​(q)A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q) the Kac polynomials of QQ counting absolutely indecomposable 𝐝\mathbf{d}-dimensional representations of QQ over 𝐅q\mathbf{F}_{q}).

This proposition is proven in [loc. cit.] by an iterative inversion of the Weyl character formula for graded GKM algebras. For the nilpotent versions of cuspidal polynomials, we have an analogue of Proposition 1.5 for the nilpotent and 11-nilpotent Kac and cuspidal polynomials. Proposition 1.5 implies that the positivity of cuspidal polynomials is a strengthening of the positivity of Kac polynomials of quivers proven in [HLR13]. Simultaneously, our results prove a strengthening of the Kac constant term conjecture [Kac83], proved originally in [Hau10]. This conjecture states that the constant terms of the Kac polynomials are equal to the root multiplicities of a certain Kac–Moody Lie algebra 𝔤Γ\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma}; we show that the entire Kac polynomial is the characteristic function of a larger (generalised) cohomologically graded Kac–Moody Lie algebra containing 𝔤Γ\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma} as its (cohomological) degree zero piece.

Our proof of the positivity of cuspidal polynomials also gives a cohomological interpretation of their coefficients.

Theorem 1.6 (Theorem 9.5).

Let 𝐝∈ΣΠQ\mathbf{d}\in\Sigma_{\Pi_{Q}}. Then,

CQ,𝐝(q)=IP(ℳΠQ,𝐝)(q−1/2).C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)=\mathrm{IP}(\mathcal{M}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathbf{d}})(q^{-1/2}).

This interpretation gives a way to calculate the intersection Poincaré polynomials of quiver varieties. The same way that Hua’s formula [Hua00] gives a way to calculate Kac polynomials by giving an effective formula for the plethystic exponential of their generating series, the above results enable us to recover the intersection Poincaré polynomials from the same series.

The intersection Poincaré polynomial of any quiver variety can be recovered using Theorem 1.6, the canonical decomposition of dimension vectors of quivers [Cra02, Theorem 1.1] which induces a decomposition of Nakajima quiver varieties [Cra02], and the formula for the intersection Poincaré polynomial of symmetric products (see Corollary 9.7 for the general result).

1.4. PBW theorems and cohomological integrality in Donaldson–Thomas theory

The BPS algebra BPS𝒜,Algψ\aBPS^{\psi}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}} is defined to be the zeroeth part of the perverse filtration on the cohomological Hall algebra H∗⁡𝒜𝒜\HO^{*}\!\mathscr{A}_{\mathcal{A}} associated to the morphism 𝙹𝙷𝒜\JH_{\mathcal{A}}, defined in [DHS22]. In particular, it is a subalgebra of H∗⁡𝒜𝒜\HO^{*}\!\mathscr{A}_{\mathcal{A}}. Theorem 1.2 completely determines the structure of this algebra, up to determining the intersection Poincaré polynomials of some singular varieties associated to simple roots (and in the case 𝒜=Rep⁡ΠQ\mathcal{A}=\operatorname{Rep}\Pi_{Q} this can be done algorithmically using absolutely cuspidal polynomials, as explained in §1.3).

Although Theorem 1.2 only concerns a subalgebra of the CoHA, we can use the same techniques to write down an explicit PBW isomorphism for the entire CoHA. To start with, in §8.3.2 we prove a stronger, “relative” PBW isomorphism in the category of complexes of mixed Hodge modules on the coarse moduli space ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}:

Theorem 1.7 (Relative PBW isomorphism).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a 22-Calabi–Yau Abelian category satisfying the assumptions of §4. After choosing a positive determinant line bundle det:𝔐𝒜→B⁡𝐂∗\det\colon\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\B\mathbf{C}^{*}, we have a canonical isomorphism

Ψ𝒜ψ:Sym⊡⁡(ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie⊗H∗⁡(B⁡𝐂∗,𝐐¯))→≅𝒜¯𝒜ψ\Psi^{\psi}_{\mathcal{A}}\colon\Sym_{\boxdot}\left(\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}\otimes\HO^{*}(\B\mathbf{C}^{*},\underline{\mathbf{Q}})\right)\xrightarrow{\cong}\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi}

of complexes of mixed Hodge modules in 𝒟+​(MHM⁡(ℳ𝒜))\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}})), with ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}} defined as in (1.1). The isomorphism is obtained by evaluating symmetric tensors in ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie⊗H∗⁡(B⁡𝐂∗,𝐐¯)\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}\otimes\HO^{*}(\B\mathbf{C}^{*},\underline{\mathbf{Q}}) using the (ψ\psi-twisted) Hall algebra structure on the target.

See §8.3.2 for the definition of a positive determinant bundle. Applying the restriction functor ı△!\imath_{\triangle}^{!} and taking derived global sections, we obtain the following corollary.

Corollary 1.8 (PBW isomorphism).

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a 22-Calabi–Yau Abelian category satisfying the assumptions of §4. Let 𝒜△⊆𝒜\mathcal{A}^{\triangle}\subseteq\mathcal{A} be a Serre subcategory. After choosing a positive determinant line bundle, we have a canonical PBW isomorphism

H∗(ı△!Ψ𝒜ψ):Sym(𝔫¯𝒜BPS,△,+⊗H∗(B𝐂∗,𝐐¯))→≅H∗𝒜¯𝒜△,ψ=HBM(𝔐𝒜△,𝐐¯vir)\HO^{*}(\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\Psi^{\psi}_{\mathcal{A}})\colon\Sym\!\left(\underline{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle,+}_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\HO^{*}(\B\mathbf{C}^{*},\underline{\mathbf{Q}})\right)\xrightarrow{\cong}\HO^{*}\!\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle,\psi}=\HO^{\BoMo}(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle},\underline{\mathbf{Q}}^{\mathrm{vir}})

of K⁡(𝒜)×𝐙\K(\mathcal{A})\times\mathbf{Z}-graded mixed Hodge structures, with 𝔫¯𝒜BPS,△,+\underline{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle,+}_{\mathcal{A}} defined as in (1.2). This isomorphism is obtained via the inclusion of cohomologically graded mixed Hodge structures 𝔫¯𝒜BPS,△,+⊗H∗⁡(B⁡𝐂∗,𝐐)↪H∗⁡𝒜¯𝒜△,ψ\underline{\mathfrak{n}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle,+}_{\mathcal{A}}\otimes\HO^{*}(\B\mathbf{C}^{*},\mathbf{Q})\hookrightarrow\HO^{*}\!\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle,\psi} determined by our choice of determinant line bundle, and the evaluation of symmetric tensors using the (ψ\psi-twisted) cohomological Hall algebra structure on the target.

As usual, we emphasize that the isomorphisms of Theorem 1.7 and Corollary 1.8 are not algebra morphisms, although both sides have their own algebra structure. The left-hand sides have the algebra structures given by the Sym\Sym construction while the right-hand sides have the cohomological Hall algebra structure. However, the isomorphism Ψ𝒜ψ\Psi^{\psi}_{\mathcal{A}} is constructed using the algebra structure on 𝒜¯𝒜ψ\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi}. This is similar to the usual PBW theorem for enveloping algebras, which gives an isomorphism, after passing to underlying vector spaces, between a polynomial algebra and the enveloping algebra.

If we choose 𝒜\mathcal{A} to be the 2-Calabi–Yau category of ΠQ\Pi_{Q}-representations, the existence of some cohomological integrality isomorphism as in Theorem 1.7 and Corollary 1.8 is (via dimensional reduction [Dav17a]) a particular case of the PBW isomorphism of Davison–Meinhardt (see [DM20], then [Dav23a]), and purity of the BPS sheaf is one of the main results of [Dav20]. However, even in this case, the precise determination of the IC complexes making up the BPS sheaf is a new result.

1.4.1. Donaldson–Thomas theory

The main application of Corollary 1.8 in enumerative geometry concerns the cohomological Donaldson–Thomas (DT) theory of local K3 surfaces, which we explain here. To start with, let XX be a projective 3CY variety, meaning that XX is smooth, three-dimensional, and has trivial canonical bundle, 𝒪X≅KX\mathscr{O}_{X}\cong K_{X}. Donaldson–Thomas theory, as introduced in [Tho00], assigns numbers to certain (fine) moduli schemes ℳ\mathcal{M} of coherent sheaves on XX, using perfect obstruction theories to produce a degree zero virtual fundamental class of ℳ\mathcal{M}. Thomas then defines #DT​(ℳ)\#_{\DT}(\mathcal{M}) to be the degree of this class. This theory was subsequently generalised in multiple directions. Firstly it was proved by Behrend [Beh09] that the count #DT​(ℳ)\#_{\DT}(\mathcal{M}) could be calculated as a weighted Euler characteristic of a certain constructible function νℳ\nu_{\mathcal{M}} (the Behrend function), so that it makes sense to define this number even if ℳ\mathcal{M} is not projective. In particular, we can replace XX with a local K3 surface. Secondly, via the papers of Joyce–Song [JS12] and Kontsevich–Soibelman [KS08], a theory was developed that removed the need to study only fine moduli spaces ℳ\mathcal{M}, i.e. stacks 𝔐\mathfrak{M}, possibly containing strictly semistable objects, are handled by their theory. Finally, an effective theory of DT mixed Hodge modules on stacks of objects in 3CY categories was developed in the sequence of papers [Bra+15, BBJ19, Ben+15]; associated to a moduli stack 𝔐\mathfrak{M} of objects in a 3CY category 𝒜\mathcal{A}, equipped with an orientation in the sense of [Joy15], they define the mixed Hodge module ϕDT\phi_{\DT}, the pointwise Euler characteristic of which is equal to the Behrend function. We recover the weighted Euler characteristics (where they make sense) by taking actual Euler characteristics of derived global sections of ϕDT\phi_{\DT}.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a 2CY category with a good moduli space, satisfying the assumptions of §4. A motivating example for us comes from setting 𝒜\mathcal{A} to be the category of Gieseker semistable coherent sheaves, of fixed slope, on a polarised K3 surface SS. In order to obtain a 3CY category, we take the 3CY completion 𝒜~=Π3​(𝒜)\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}=\Pi_{3}(\mathcal{A}) in the sense of [Kel11]. It is shown in [BCS20] that the shifted cotangent stack 𝕸~m=T∗⁡[−1]​𝕸m\bm{\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}}_{m}=\T^{*}[-1]\bm{\mathfrak{M}}_{m} is equivalent to a substack of the (derived) stack of objects in 𝒜~\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}. Being the classical truncation of a (−1)(-1)-shifted cotangent stack, 𝔐~m=t0​(𝕸~m)\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_{m}=t_{0}(\bm{\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}}_{m}) carries a canonical orientation, and indeed a canonical d-critical structure, determining the mixed Hodge module ϕDT\phi_{\DT} on it; see [Kin22] for the details. In [loc. cit] it is moreover proved that there is a canonical dimensional reduction isomorphism, for each m∈K⁡(𝒜)m\in\K(\mathcal{A}):

H⁡(𝔐~m,ϕDT)≅HBM⁡(𝔐m,𝐐vir)\HO(\widetilde{\mathfrak{M}}_{m},\phi_{\DT})\cong\HO^{\BoMo}(\mathfrak{M}_{m},\mathbf{Q}^{\mathrm{vir}})

where the vir\mathrm{vir} superscript denotes a system of Tate twists that we do not make explicit in this introduction.

A foundational/definitional conjecture in Donaldson–Thomas theory is the integrality conjecture. In the enumerative version of the theory this is the claim that certain partition functions with coefficients given by DT invariants are obtained by taking plethystic exponentials of partition functions involving simpler invariants, called BPS invariants: see [KS08] for an exact formulation in the enumerative setup. This enumerative version is implied by a stronger cohomological version of the integrality theorem:

Conjecture 1.9.

Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a 3CY Abelian category on which the Euler form vanishes and cl:π0​(𝔐𝒞)→K⁡(𝒞)\mathrm{cl}\colon\pi_{0}(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{C}})\rightarrow\K(\mathcal{C}) is a surjective morphism to a monoid. Then there is some isomorphism of K⁡(𝒞)\K(\mathcal{C})-graded, cohomologically graded mixed Hodge structures

⨁m∈K⁡(𝒞)H⁡(𝔐𝒞,m,ϕ¯DT)≅Sym⁡(⨁0≠m∈K⁡(𝒞)BPS¯𝒞,m⊗H⁡(B⁡𝐂∗,𝐐¯))\bigoplus_{m\in\K(\mathcal{C})}\HO(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{C},m},\underline{\phi}_{\DT})\cong\Sym\left(\bigoplus_{0\neq m\in\K(\mathcal{C})}\underline{\aBPS}_{\mathcal{C},m}\otimes\HO(\B\mathbf{C}^{*},\underline{\mathbf{Q}})\right)

where each BPS¯𝒞,m\underline{\aBPS}_{\mathcal{C},m} has bounded cohomological amplitude, and finite total dimension.

Via dimensional reduction, we obtain the following from Theorem 1.7.

Theorem 1.10.

Conjecture 1.9 is true for 3CY categories of the form 𝒜~=Π3​(𝒜)\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}=\Pi_{3}(\mathcal{A}) for 𝒜\mathcal{A} a 2-Calabi–Yau category satisfying the assumptions of §4. In particular, if X=Tot⁡(KS)≅S×𝐀1X=\operatorname{Tot}(K_{S})\cong S\times\mathbf{A}^{1} for SS a smooth quasiprojective surface satisfying KS≅𝒪S\K_{S}\cong\mathscr{O}_{S}, the cohomological integrality conjecture holds for the category of Gieseker semistable11 1 With respect to a polarisation of a compactification of SS. compactly supported coherent sheaves of fixed slope on XX.

In the case 𝒜=𝐇𝐢𝐠𝐠𝐬θ​(C)\mathcal{A}=\mathbf{Higgs}_{\theta}(C), the category of semistable Higgs sheaves of fixed slope θ\theta on a smooth projective curve CC, 𝒜~=Π3​(𝒜)\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}=\Pi_{3}(\mathcal{A}) can be identified with the category of semistable coherent sheaves of pure dimension one on TotC⁡(𝒪C⊕KC)\operatorname{Tot}_{C}(\mathscr{O}_{C}\oplus K_{C}), and Conjecture 1.9 is proved in [KK21], building on [KM21, MS20]. In the case in which g⁡(C)⩾2g(C)\geqslant 2, the precise determination of BPS¯𝒜~\underline{\aBPS}_{\widetilde{\mathcal{A}}} in terms of intersection cohomology was obtained in our earlier work [DHS22], while for g⁡(C)⩽1g(C)\leqslant 1 it can be found in [Dav23].

Remark 1.11.

We may alternatively define BPS¯𝒞,m≔H⁡(ℳ𝒞,m,ℋ1​((𝔐𝒞→ℳ𝒞)∗​ϕ¯DT))\underline{\aBPS}_{\mathcal{C},m}\coloneqq\HO(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{C},m},\mathcal{H}^{1}((\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{C}}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{C}})_{*}\underline{\phi}_{\DT})) and make the stronger conjecture that for this choice of mixed Hodge structure, there is an isomorphism as in Conjecture 1.9. The local version of this conjecture (for Jacobi algebras) is the main result of [DM20]; see §1.6 for this special case. Proving this stronger version of the integrality conjecture is beyond the scope of the current paper, and forms the subject of an upcoming paper by the first-named author and Tasuki Kinjo.

1.5. Lowest weight modules from Nakajima quiver varieties

Part of the inspiration for constructing generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebras out of 2CY categories was the famous work of Nakajima on irreducible highest/lowest weight representations constructed out of cohomology of quiver varieties, and work of Nakajima and Grojnowski on irreducible highest/lowest weight representations of Heisenberg algebras on cohomology of Hilbert schemes. In this section we explain how we recover and extend this theory.

Given a quiver QQ without loops, and a framing dimension vector 𝐟∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{f}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}, Nakajima constructs in [Nak98] an action of the Kac–Moody Lie algebra 𝔤Γ\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma} on ⨁𝐝∈𝐍Q0H0⁡(N⁡(Q,𝐝,𝐟),𝐐vir)\bigoplus_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}}\HO^{0}(N(Q,\mathbf{d},\mathbf{f}),\mathbf{Q}^{\mathrm{vir}}) where Γ\Gamma is the underlying graph of QQ, 𝔤Γ\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma} is the associated Kac–Moody Lie algebra, and N⁡(Q,𝐝,𝐟)N(Q,\mathbf{d},\mathbf{f}) are Nakajima quiver varieties (we recall the definition in §10.2, along with the cohomological shifts bundled into the superscript vir\mathrm{vir}). Furthermore, this representation is shown to be the irreducible lowest weight representation of lowest weight ∑i∈Q0fi​δi\sum_{i\in Q_{0}}f_{i}\delta_{i}, where the δi\delta_{i}s denote the fundamental weights. Note that the same correspondences considered in [Nak98] act on the entire cohomology 𝕄𝐟​(Q)≔⨁𝐝∈𝐍Q0H∗⁡(N⁡(Q,𝐝,𝐟),𝐐vir)\mathbb{M}_{\mathbf{f}}(Q)\coloneqq\bigoplus_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}}\HO^{*}(N(Q,\mathbf{d},\mathbf{f}),\mathbf{Q}^{\mathrm{vir}}), suggesting the following question:

Question 1.12.

For fixed QQ and 𝐟∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{f}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}, what is the decomposition of the entire cohomology 𝕄𝐟​(Q)\mathbb{M}_{\mathbf{f}}(Q) into irreducible lowest weight 𝔤Γ\mathfrak{g}_{\Gamma}-modules?

Next, let QQ be instead the Jordan quiver; this is the quiver with one vertex and one loop. We fix the framing vector f=1f=1; then there is an isomorphism N⁡(Q,d,1)≅Hilbd⁡(𝐀2)N(Q,d,1)\cong\Hilb_{d}(\mathbf{A}^{2}). Again, 𝕄1​(Q)\mathbb{M}_{1}(Q) is acted on by an algebra of correspondences (Nakajima’s raising and lowering operators), and it is proved in [Nak97, Nak99] that the resulting Lie algebra of correspondences 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is an infinite-dimensional Heisenberg algebra. Moreover, it is proven that 𝕄1​(Q)\mathbb{M}_{1}(Q) is an irreducible lowest weight module for this Lie algebra. Note that this is a long way from being a special case of the result in the paragraph above Question 1.12, since QQ only contains a loop. On the other hand, the algebra 𝔤\mathfrak{g} is a (very degenerate example of a) generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra, containing only imaginary simple roots.

These two central results in the geometric representation theory of quiver varieties motivate the following more ambitious question:

Question 1.13.

For fixed QQ, is there a natural generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra 𝔤~Q\widetilde{\mathfrak{g}}_{Q} of correspondences, containing the Kac–Moody Lie algebra associated to the real subquiver (see §2), for which, for fixed 𝐟∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{f}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}, the module 𝕄𝐟​(Q)\mathbb{M}_{\mathbf{f}}(Q) admits a concrete decomposition into irreducible lowest weight modules?

Although Question 1.13 is more subjective, we still venture to answer it with a “yes” in this paper. Firstly, we propose the (full) BPS Lie algebra 𝔤ΠQBPS\mathfrak{g}^{\mathtt{\aBPS}}_{\Pi_{Q}} introduced at (1.4) to be the Lie algebra 𝔤~Q\widetilde{\mathfrak{g}}_{Q}. Then the decomposition into irreducible lowest weight representations, with lowest weight spaces identified with intersection cohomology of certain singular moduli spaces of framed representations, is provided by the following theorem, a more general version of which is proved as Theorem 10.5:

Theorem 1.14.

The 𝔫ΠQBPS,+\mathfrak{n}_{\Pi_{Q}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},+}-action on 𝕄𝐟​(Q)\mathbb{M}_{\mathbf{f}}(Q) extends to a 𝔤ΠQBPS\mathfrak{g}_{\Pi_{Q}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS}}-action, for which 𝕄𝐟​(Q)\mathbb{M}_{\mathbf{f}}(Q) decomposes as a direct sum of cohomologically shifted simple lowest weight representations, with lowest weight spaces identified with intersection cohomology of singular quiver varieties:

𝕄𝐟​(Q)≅⨁(𝐝,1)∈ΦQ𝐟+IH^*⁡(ℳΠQ𝐟,(𝐝,1))⊗L((𝐝,1),(−,0))Q𝐟.\mathbb{M}_{\mathbf{f}}(Q)\cong\bigoplus_{(\mathbf{d},1)\in\Phi_{Q_{\mathbf{f}}}^{+}}\ICA\!(\mathcal{M}_{\Pi_{Q_{\mathbf{f}}},(\mathbf{d},1)})\otimes L_{((\mathbf{d},1),(-,0))_{Q_{\mathbf{f}}}}.

Here, IH^*\ICA denotes the result of the derived global section functor applied to the perverse IC complex.

We explain how to recover the above results of [Nak97, Nak98, Gro96] from Theorem 10.5 in §10.4.

Remark 1.15.

A consequence of our results is that 𝔤ΠQBPS\mathfrak{g}_{\Pi_{Q}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS}}acts faithfully on the direct sum of modules 𝕄𝐟​(Q)\mathbb{M}_{\mathbf{f}}(Q) provided by taking the cohomology of Nakajima quiver varieties for various framing vectors 𝐟\mathbf{f}. In [MO19] Maulik and Okounkov associate to each quiver QQ a Lie algebra 𝔤𝙼𝙾,Q\mathfrak{g}_{\mathtt{MO},Q} (after extending scalars from 𝐐\mathbf{Q} to an equivariant cohomology ring). By construction, their Lie algebra acts faithfully on cohomology of Nakajima quiver varieties, and admits a 𝐙Q0\mathbf{Z}^{Q_{0}}-graded weight space decomposition. Furthermore, 𝔤𝙼𝙾,Q\mathfrak{g}_{\mathtt{MO},Q} is conjectured to be a generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra, is conjectured to be already defined over 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, and is known to contain the usual Kac–Moody Lie algebra associated to QQ. The main results of this paper, then, should be taken as strong evidence for the conjectures22 2 These conjectures have now been proved in [BD23]. The proof uses in an essential way the description of the BPS Lie algebra as a generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra which forms Theorem 1.2, as well as the description of its representation theory contained in Theorem 1.14. These conjectures in turn imply Okounkov’s conjecture equating the graded dimensions of 𝔤𝙼𝙾,Q\mathfrak{g}_{\mathtt{MO},Q} with coefficients of Kac polynomials, see [BD23, SV23]. (in [MO19] and [Dav20] respectively) that 𝔤𝙼𝙾,Q\mathfrak{g}_{\mathtt{MO},Q} can be defined over 𝐐\mathbf{Q}, and (after extending scalars) there is an isomorphism 𝔫ΠQBPS,+≅𝔫𝙼𝙾,Q+\mathfrak{n}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},+}_{\Pi_{Q}}\cong\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathtt{MO},Q}.

1.6. Comparison with the 3d BPS Lie algebra

If 𝒜=Rep⁡ΠQ\mathcal{A}=\operatorname{Rep}\Pi_{Q}, a definition of the BPS Lie algebra sheaf associated to the vanishing cycle cohomology of the stack of ΠQ​[x]\Pi_{Q}[x]-modules is given in [Dav20] using the fact that ΠQ​[x]\Pi_{Q}[x] is the 33-Calabi–Yau Jacobi algebra associated to a quiver with potential. CoHAs for vanishing cycle cohomology of Jacobi algebras were defined and studied in [KS11]. We denote this BPS Lie algebra sheaf by ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie𝟹​𝚍,ψ∈Perv⁡(ℳΠQ)\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}^{\mathtt{3d},\psi}\in\operatorname{Perv}(\mathcal{M}_{\Pi_{Q}}). The superscript 𝟹​𝚍\mathtt{3d} indicates that the definition involves dimensional reduction from the stack of representations of a Jacobi algebra. This sheaf is the direct image of the BPS sheaf defined in the context of quivers with potential in [DM20], and this approach to defining BPS sheaves is very much inspired by the theory recalled in §1.4.1.

Although the BPS Lie algebra sheaf (for an arbitrary 2CY category) in this paper is defined very differently, for the category of ΠQ\Pi_{Q}-modules we nonetheless prove the following in §8.2 (Proposition 8.4):

Theorem 1.16.

Let QQ be a quiver. The relative BPS Lie algebras ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}} and ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie𝟹​𝚍,ψ\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}^{\mathtt{3d},\psi} are canonically isomorphic.

In particular, the BPS Lie algebra sheaf ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie𝟹​𝚍,ψ\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}^{\mathtt{3d},\psi} is (up to isomorphism) independent of the chosen ψ\psi-twist. We expect Theorem 1.16 to be true for general 3CY completions of 2CY categories (see upcoming work of the first-named author and Tasuki Kinjo).

2. Quivers and representations

A quiver is a directed graph, i.e. a pair of sets Q1Q_{1} and Q0Q_{0} of arrows and vertices, respectively, along with a pair of maps s,t:Q1→Q0s,t\colon Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0} taking an arrow to its source and target, respectively.

We allow our quivers to have loops (i.e. 1-cycles). Let Q0im⊆Q0Q_{0}^{\mathrm{im}}\subseteq Q_{0} be the subset of vertices supporting loops, which we call imaginary vertices. We denote by Q⊆QQ\subseteq Q the quiver obtained by replacing Q0Q_{0} with Q0∖Q0imQ_{0}\smallsetminus Q_{0}^{\mathrm{im}}, and removing all arrows from Q1Q_{1} that have source or target in Q0imQ_{0}^{\mathrm{im}}.

We denote by

χQ​(−,−):\displaystyle\chi_{Q}(-,-)\colon 𝐙Q0×𝐙Q0→𝐙\displaystyle\mathbf{Z}^{Q_{0}}\times\mathbf{Z}^{Q_{0}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}
(𝐝′,𝐝′′)↦∑i∈Q0di′​di′′−∑a∈Q1ds⁡(a)′​dt⁡(a)′′\displaystyle(\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime})\mapsto\sum_{i\in Q_{0}}d^{\prime}_{i}d^{\prime\prime}_{i}-\sum_{a\in Q_{1}}d^{\prime}_{s(a)}d^{\prime\prime}_{t(a)}

the Euler form of QQ, and define (−,−)Q(-,-)_{Q} to be its symmetrisation. For 𝐝′,𝐝′′∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}, we define the dot product by 𝐝′⋅𝐝′′=∑i∈Q0di′​di′′\mathbf{d}^{\prime}\cdot\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime}=\sum_{i\in Q_{0}}d^{\prime}_{i}d^{\prime\prime}_{i}.

Given a quiver QQ we denote by 𝐂​Q\mathbf{C}Q the free path algebra, i.e. the algebra having a 𝐂\mathbf{C}-basis given by paths in QQ, including paths 𝒆i\bm{e}_{i} of length zero at each of the vertices ii. The multiplication, with respect to this basis, is given by concatenation of paths.

If A=𝐂​Q/RA=\mathbf{C}Q/R is presented as the quotient of a free path algebra by a two sided ideal generated by linear combinations of paths of length of at least one, and ρ\rho is an AA-module, we define the dimension vector

dimQ0(ρ)≔(dim(𝒆i⋅ρ))i∈Q0∈𝐍Q0.\dim_{Q_{0}}(\rho)\coloneqq(\dim(\bm{e}_{i}\!\cdot\!\rho))_{i\in Q_{0}}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}.

For a quiver QQ and dimension vector 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} we define

𝐀Q,𝐝≔∏a∈Q1Hom⁡(𝐂ds⁡(a),𝐂dt⁡(a))\mathbf{A}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}\coloneqq\prod_{a\in Q_{1}}\operatorname{Hom}(\mathbf{C}^{d_{s(a)}},\mathbf{C}^{d_{t(a)}})

which is acted on by the gauge group

GL𝐝≔∏i∈Q0GLdi​(𝐂)\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbf{d}}\coloneqq\prod_{i\in Q_{0}}\mathrm{GL}_{d_{i}}(\mathbf{C})

by change of basis. 3. Generalized Kac–Moody algebras

In this section, we give the constructions of the generalised Kac–Moody algebra associated to a monoid with bilinear form and a weight function following [Bor88], and of generalised half Kac–Moody algebras in symmetric tensor categories of mixed Hodge modules/perverse sheaves. We work with monoids with bilinear forms to allow sufficient flexibility when investigating the BPS algebras of 22-Calabi–Yau categories.

3.1. Roots

3.1.1. Primitive and positive roots

Let (M,+)(M,+) be a monoid and M×M→𝐙M\times M\rightarrow\mathbf{Z} be a bilinear form. When considering Weyl group actions we assume that MM is finitely generated, commutative, torsion-free, and cancellative; equivalently, we require that the natural map M→M^M\rightarrow\widehat{M} to the groupification is injective, and M^\widehat{M} is a lattice. All definitions of roots make sense without these assumptions (which may not be satisfied by the monoid of connected components of the good moduli space of 2CY categories). We let

(3.1) ΣM,(−,−)={m∈M∣2−(m,m)⩾0 and 2−(m,m)>∑j=1s(2−(mj,mj)) for any nontrivial decomposition m=∑j=1smj with mj∈M∖{0}}\Sigma_{M,(-,-)}=\left\{m\in M\mid 2-(m,m)\geqslant 0\text{ and }2-(m,m)>\sum_{j=1}^{s}(2-(m_{j},m_{j}))\right.\\ \left.\text{ for any nontrivial decomposition $m=\sum_{j=1}^{s}m_{j}$ with $m_{j}\in M\smallsetminus\{0\}$}\right\}

be the set of primitive positive roots, and

ΦM,(−,−)+=ΣM,(−,−)∪{lm∣l∈𝐍⩾1,m∈ΣM,(−,−) and (m,m)=0}\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}=\Sigma_{M,(-,-)}\cup\{lm\mid l\in\mathbf{N}_{\geqslant 1},m\in\Sigma_{M,(-,-)}\text{ and }(m,m)=0\}

be the set of simple positive roots. We assume that (m,m)∈2​𝐙⩽1(m,m)\in 2\mathbf{Z}_{\leqslant 1} for m∈ΦM,(−,−)+m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}. We write the decomposition of ΦM,(−,−)+\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+} into real and imaginary roots, ΦM,(−,−)+=ΦM,(−,−)+,⊔ΦM,(−,−)+,im\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}=\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\real}\sqcup\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\mathrm{im}}, where ΦM,(−,−)+,≔{m∈ΦM,(−,−)+∣(m,m)=2}\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\real}\coloneqq\{m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}\mid(m,m)=2\} and ΦM,(−,−)+,im≔{m∈ΦM,(−,−)+∣(m,m)⩽0}\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\mathrm{im}}\coloneqq\{m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}\mid(m,m)\leqslant 0\}. We can further decompose ΦM,(−,−)+,im=ΦM,(−,−)+,iso⊔ΦM,(−,−)+,hyp\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\mathrm{im}}=\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\mathrm{iso}}\sqcup\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\mathrm{hyp}} where

ΦM,(−,−)+,iso≔{m∈ΦM,(−,−)+∣(m,m)=0}\displaystyle\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\mathrm{iso}}\coloneqq\{m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}\mid(m,m)=0\}
ΦM,(−,−)+,hyp≔{m∈ΦM,(−,−)+∣(m,m)<0}\displaystyle\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\mathrm{hyp}}\coloneqq\{m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}\mid(m,m)<0\}

are the sets of isotropic and hyperbolic roots, respectively. For m∈ΦM,(−,−)+,iso∩ΣM,(−,−)m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\mathrm{iso}}\cap\Sigma_{M,(-,-)} we call mm an indivisible isotropic root.

We fix an Abelian category 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and an ambient dg subcategory 𝒞\mathscr{C} which contains 𝒜\mathcal{A} as a subcategory of its homotopy category, and a fixed stack of objects 𝔐𝒜\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}} in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, such that the Euler form (−,−)𝒞(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}} is locally constant on 𝔐𝒜×𝔐𝒜\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\times\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}. We assume that we have a chosen monoid K⁡(𝒜)\K(\mathcal{A}) and a fixed surjective morphism of monoids

π0​(𝔐𝒜)→K⁡(𝒜).\pi_{0}(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}})\rightarrow\K(\mathcal{A}).

As in §2 we assume that the natural morphism to the groupification K⁡(𝒜)→K⁡(𝒜)^\K(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\widehat{\K(\mathcal{A})} is injective, K⁡(𝒜)^\widehat{\K(\mathcal{A})} is a lattice, and the Euler form (−,−)𝒞(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}} descends to a bilinear form on K⁡(𝒜)\K(\mathcal{A}) (and thus induces a bilinear form on K⁡(𝒜)^\widehat{\K(\mathcal{A})}). We denote by ΣK⁡(𝒜)\Sigma_{\K(\mathcal{A})} and ΦK⁡(𝒜)+\Phi_{\K(\mathcal{A})}^{+} the sets of primitive positive roots and simple positive roots, respectively, associated to the monoid K⁡(𝒜)\K(\mathcal{A}) endowed with the Euler form.

Remark 3.1.

The hypotheses on (m,m)(m,m) and the definition of ΦM,(−,−)+,\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+,\real} are designed for the study of the BPS algebras of 22-Calabi–Yau categories. It is certainly possible to weaken or generalise them to combinatorially define a broader class of GKM algebras. A possible different choice would be

(3.2) ΦM,(−,−)+,≔{m∈M∣(m,m)>0}\displaystyle\Phi^{+,\real}_{M,(-,-)}\coloneqq\{m\in M\mid(m,m)>0\}
(3.3) 2​(m,n)(m,m)∈𝐙⩽0​ if m∈ΦM,(−,−)+, and n∈ΦM,(−,−)+.\displaystyle\frac{2(m,n)}{(m,m)}\in\mathbf{Z}_{\leqslant 0}\text{ if $m\in\Phi^{+,\real}_{M,(-,-)}$ and $n\in\Phi^{+}_{M,(-,-)}$}.

This would be useful if we had positive roots mm with (m,m)>2(m,m)>2 but this is not the case for 2CY categories.

Lemma 3.2.

Let f:M→Nf\colon M\rightarrow N be a surjective morphism of monoids, and let (−,−)M(-,-)_{M} and (−,−)N(-,-)_{N} be bilinear forms on M,NM,N respectively such that f∗​(−,−)N=(−,−)Mf^{*}(-,-)_{N}=(-,-)_{M}. We assume that f⁡(m)≠0f(m)\neq 0 if m∈ΣM,(−,−)Mm\in\Sigma_{M,(-,-)_{M}}. Then, f−1​(ΣN,(−,−)N)=ΣM,(−,−)Mf^{-1}(\Sigma_{N,(-,-)_{N}})=\Sigma_{M,(-,-)_{M}}.

Proof.

This is straightforward from the definitions of the sets of primitive positive roots. ∎

For example, one may take for MM the monoid of connected components of the good moduli space of objects in a category (§4).

3.3. Lowest weight modules

Let (M,(−,−))(M,(-,-)) be a monoid with bilinear form. We assume that the natural map M→M^M\rightarrow\widehat{M} is an embedding into a lattice. V𝔤,𝐟≔𝐔⁡(𝔤)⊗𝐔⁡(𝔟−)𝐂,V_{\mathfrak{g},\mathbf{f}}\coloneqq\UEA(\mathfrak{g})\otimes_{\UEA(\mathfrak{b}^{-})}\mathbf{C},

where 𝐂\mathbf{C} is a 𝐔⁡(𝔟−)\UEA(\mathfrak{b}^{-})-module via the quotient 𝐔⁡(𝔟−)→𝐔⁡(𝔥)\UEA(\mathfrak{b}^{-})\rightarrow\UEA(\mathfrak{h}) and the action of 𝔥\mathfrak{h} on 𝐂\mathbf{C} is given by hm⋅1≔𝐟⁡(m)h_{m}\cdot 1\coloneqq\mathbf{f}(m) for m∈Mm\in M. We let v≔1⊗1∈V𝔤,𝐟v\coloneqq 1\otimes 1\in V_{\mathfrak{g},\mathbf{f}}. There is a unique maximal submodule of V𝔤,𝐟V_{\mathfrak{g},\mathbf{f}} not containing vv. We denote by L𝔤,𝐟L_{\mathfrak{g},\mathbf{f}} (or L𝐟L_{\mathbf{f}} for short) the quotient of V𝔤,𝐟V_{\mathfrak{g},\mathbf{f}} by this submodule. It is a simple 𝔤\mathfrak{g}-module. It is called the simple lowest weight 𝔤\mathfrak{g}-module of weight 𝐟\mathbf{f}.

3.4. Cartan involution

The Cartan involution of 𝔤M,(−,−),P\mathfrak{g}_{M,(-,-),P} is the unique automorphism of Lie algebras w:𝔤M,(−,−),P→𝔤M,(−,−),Pw\colon\mathfrak{g}_{M,(-,-),P}\rightarrow\mathfrak{g}_{M,(-,-),P} such that for any m∈ΦM,(−,−)+m\in\Phi^{+}_{M,(-,-)}, j∈𝐙j\in\mathbf{Z}, 1⩽l⩽pm,j1\leqslant l\leqslant p_{m,j},

w⁡(em,j,l)=−fm,j,l\displaystyle w(e_{m,j,l})=-f_{m,j,l}
w⁡(fm,j,l)=−em,j,l\displaystyle w(f_{m,j,l})=-e_{m,j,l}
w⁡(hm)=−hm.\displaystyle w(h_{m})=-h_{m}.

It is described for Kac–Moody algebras in [Kac90, §1.3]. For generalised Kac–Moody algebras, its definition appears in [Bor88, §1].

3.5. Generalised half Kac–Moody (Lie) algebras in tensor categories of mixed Hodge modules or perverse sheaves

We let (ℳ,⊕)(\mathcal{M},\oplus) be a commutative monoid in the category of complex schemes. We allow ℳ\mathcal{M} to have infinitely many connected components. We assume that each connected component of ℳ\mathcal{M} is a finite type separated scheme and that the sum ⊕:ℳ×ℳ→ℳ\oplus\colon\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{M} is a finite morphism. The formula ℱ⊡𝒢≔⊕∗(ℱ⊠𝒢)\mathscr{F}\boxdot\mathscr{G}\coloneqq\oplus_{*}(\mathscr{F}\boxtimes\mathscr{G}) defines symmetric monoidal structures on 𝒟c+​(ℳ)\mathcal{D}^{+}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathcal{M}) and 𝒟+​(MHM​(ℳ))\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M})), and by tt-exactness of ⊕∗\oplus_{*}, also on Perv⁡(ℳ)\operatorname{Perv}(\mathcal{M}) and MHM⁡(ℳ)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}). We let Tℱ,𝒢:ℱ⊡𝒢→≅𝒢⊡ℱT_{\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G}}\colon\mathscr{F}\boxdot\mathscr{G}\xrightarrow{\cong}\mathscr{G}\boxdot\mathscr{F} be the natural isomorphisms for objects ℱ,𝒢\mathscr{F},\mathscr{G} of 𝒟cb​(ℳ)\mathcal{D}^{\mathrm{b}}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathcal{M}) or 𝒟+​(MHM​(ℳ))\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M})). See [MSS11] for details. In this section, we define (positive halves of) generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebras in the tensor category MHM⁡(ℳ)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}). The same formulas provide a definition for generalised half Kac–Moody Lie algebras in Perv⁡(ℳ)\operatorname{Perv}(\mathcal{M}); we do not make them explicit (just apply the functor 𝐫𝐚𝐭:MHM⁡(ℳ)→Perv⁡(ℳ)\mathbf{rat}\colon\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M})\rightarrow\operatorname{Perv}(\mathcal{M})).

3.5.3. Enveloping algebras

If ℒ¯\underline{\mathscr{L}} is a Lie algebra object in MHM⁡(ℳ)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}), we let Free⊡-Alg⁡(ℒ¯)\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{L}}) be the free associative algebra generated by the underlying mixed Hodge module of ℒ¯\underline{\mathscr{L}} defined in §3.5.1. We let 𝐔⁡(ℒ¯)\UEA(\underline{\mathscr{L}}) be the quotient of Free⊡-Alg⁡(ℒ¯)\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{L}}) by the two-sided ideal generated by the image of the morphism

(3.4) C≔[−,−]⊕(Tℒ¯,ℒ¯−idℒ¯⊡ℒ¯):ℒ¯⊡ℒ¯→ℒ¯⊕(ℒ¯⊡ℒ¯)⊆Free⊡-Alg⁡(ℒ¯).C\coloneqq[-,-]\oplus(T_{\underline{\mathscr{L}},\underline{\mathscr{L}}}-\operatorname{id}_{\underline{\mathscr{L}}\boxdot\underline{\mathscr{L}}})\colon\underline{\mathscr{L}}\boxdot\underline{\mathscr{L}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{L}}\oplus(\underline{\mathscr{L}}\boxdot\underline{\mathscr{L}})\subseteq\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{L}}).

We have a canonical monomorphism of Lie algebra objects ℒ¯→𝐔⁡(ℒ¯)\underline{\mathscr{L}}\rightarrow\UEA(\underline{\mathscr{L}}) induced by the canonical inclusion ℒ¯→Free⊡-Alg⁡(ℒ¯)\underline{\mathscr{L}}\rightarrow\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{L}}), considering the target as a Lie algebra via the commutator bracket.

Proposition 3.3 (Universal property).

For any associative algebra 𝒜¯\underline{\mathscr{A}} in (MHM⁡(ℳ),⊡)(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}),\boxdot) and any morphism of Lie algebras ℒ¯→𝒜¯\underline{\mathscr{L}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}, there exists a unique morphism of algebras 𝐔⁡(ℒ¯)→𝒜¯\UEA(\underline{\mathscr{L}})\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}} such that the following diagram commutes:
Proof.

The proof follows exactly the same steps as the proof of the analogous statement for Lie algebras and their enveloping algebras in the category of vector spaces. In brief, the morphism ℒ¯→𝒜¯\underline{\mathscr{L}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}} induces a morphism Free⊡-Alg⁡(ℒ¯)→𝒜¯\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{L}})\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}. The image of CC (3.4) is clearly in the kernel of this morphism. We then obtain the factorisation 𝐔⁡(ℒ¯)→𝒜¯\UEA(\underline{\mathscr{L}})\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}} as in the proposition. The uniqueness is immediate, as ℒ¯\underline{\mathscr{L}} generates the algebra object 𝐔⁡(ℒ¯)\UEA(\underline{\mathscr{L}}). ∎

Proposition 3.4 (PBW isomorphism).

Let ℒ¯∈MHM⁡(ℳ)\underline{\mathscr{L}}\in\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}) be a Lie algebra object. Then the morphism

Sym⊡⁡(ℒ¯)→𝐔⁡(ℒ¯)\Sym_{\boxdot}(\underline{\mathscr{L}})\rightarrow\UEA(\underline{\mathscr{L}})

induced by the multiplication is an isomorphism.

Proof.

The proof is identical to that for ordinary Lie algebras. Namely, we can define a filtration of 𝐔⁡(ℒ¯)\UEA(\underline{\mathscr{L}}) by letting 𝐔⁡(ℒ¯)n\UEA(\underline{\mathscr{L}})_{n} be the image under the canonical surjection Free⊡-Alg⁡(ℒ¯)→𝐔⁡(ℒ¯)\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{L}})\rightarrow\UEA(\underline{\mathscr{L}}) of the sub-mixed Hodge module ⨁m⩽nℒ¯⊡m\bigoplus_{m\leqslant n}\underline{\mathscr{L}}^{\boxdot m}. The corresponding associated graded algebra object is isomorphic to Sym⊡⁡(ℒ¯)\Sym_{\boxdot}(\underline{\mathscr{L}}). ∎

We now give a formal proposition whose proof follows from the universal property of the universal enveloping algebra.

Proposition 3.5.

Let 𝒢¯\underline{\mathscr{G}} be an object of the symmetric monoidal category MHM⁡(ℳ)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}). Let Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢¯)\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}) be the free Lie algebra generated by 𝒢¯\underline{\mathscr{G}} and ℛ¯⊆Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢¯)\underline{\mathscr{R}}\subseteq\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}) be a suboject. Consider the Lie ideal ℐℛ¯,Lie⊆Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢¯)\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Lie}}\subseteq\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}) generated by ℛ¯\underline{\mathscr{R}}. Consider also the two-sided ideal ℐℛ¯,Alg⊆Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯)\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Alg}}\subseteq\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}) generated by ℛ¯\underline{\mathscr{R}}. Then the universal enveloping algebra 𝐔⁡(Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢¯)/ℐℛ¯,Lie)\UEA(\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\underline{\mathscr{G}})/\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Lie}}) is naturally isomorphic to the algebra Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯)/ℐℛ¯,Alg\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}})/\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Alg}}. Moreover, the Lie subalgebra ℒ¯⊆𝐔⁡(Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢¯)/ℐℛ¯,Lie)\underline{\mathscr{L}}\subseteq\UEA(\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\underline{\mathscr{G}})/\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Lie}}) generated by 𝒢¯⊆𝐔⁡(Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢¯)/ℐℛ¯,Lie)\underline{\mathscr{G}}\subseteq\UEA(\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\underline{\mathscr{G}})/\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Lie}}) coincides with Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢¯)/ℐℛ¯,Lie\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\underline{\mathscr{G}})/\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Lie}}.

Proof.

Let 𝒜¯=Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯)/ℐℛ¯,Alg\underline{\mathscr{A}}=\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}})/\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Alg}}, 𝔫¯=Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢¯)/ℐℛ¯,Lie\underline{\mathfrak{n}}=\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\underline{\mathscr{G}})/\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Lie}} and ℬ¯=𝐔⁡(𝔫¯)\underline{\mathscr{B}}=\UEA(\underline{\mathfrak{n}}). Since ℐℛ¯,Lie⊆ℐℛ¯,Alg\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Lie}}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Alg}} we have a morphism of Lie algebras 𝔫¯→𝒜¯\underline{\mathfrak{n}}\to\underline{\mathscr{A}}. By Proposition 3.3, it extends uniquely to a morphism of algebras ℬ¯→𝒜¯\underline{\mathscr{B}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}. Conversely, we have a morphism of algebras Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢)→ℬ¯\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\mathscr{G})\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{B}} induced by the natural map 𝒢¯→ℬ¯\underline{\mathscr{G}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{B}}. The generating subobject ℛ¯\underline{\mathscr{R}} of the ideal ℐℛ¯,Alg\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Alg}} is sent to zero by this morphism since ℛ¯⊆ℐℛ¯,Lie\underline{\mathscr{R}}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Lie}}. We then obtain the morphism 𝒜¯→ℬ¯\underline{\mathscr{A}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{B}} by quotienting the source by ℐℛ¯,Alg\mathcal{I}_{\underline{\mathscr{R}},\mathrm{Alg}}. The morphisms 𝒜¯→ℬ¯\underline{\mathscr{A}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{B}} and ℬ¯→𝒜¯\underline{\mathscr{B}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}} are inverse of each other (as their composition is the identity on the generating subobject 𝒢¯\underline{\mathscr{G}}).

The second part of the statement follows from the first since both Lie algebras are generated by 𝒢¯\underline{\mathscr{G}}. ∎

Definition 3.6 (Positive part of the enveloping algebra and generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra).

We define 𝔫ℳ,(−,−),𝒢¯+≔Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢¯)/ℐℳ,𝒢¯,Lie\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},(-,-),\underline{\mathscr{G}}}\coloneqq\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\underline{\mathscr{G}})/\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{M},\underline{\mathscr{G}},\mathrm{Lie}}. It has an induced Lie algebra structure in MHM⁡(ℳ)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}). We let 𝐔⁡(𝔫ℳ,(−,−),𝒢¯+)\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},(-,-),\underline{\mathscr{G}}}) be its universal enveloping algebra in MHM⁡(ℳ)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}).

The MHM 𝐔⁡(𝔫ℳ,(−,−),𝒢¯+)\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},(-,-),\underline{\mathscr{G}}}) is an algebra object in MHM⁡(ℳ)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}) and it is isomorphic to Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯)/ℐℳ,𝒢¯,Alg\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}})/\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{M},\underline{\mathscr{G}},\mathrm{Alg}} by Proposition 3.5. By the same proposition, 𝔫ℳ,(−,−),𝒢¯+\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},(-,-),\underline{\mathscr{G}}} is the Lie subalgebra object in 𝐔⁡(𝔫ℳ,(−,−),𝒢¯+)\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},(-,-),\underline{\mathscr{G}}}) generated by 𝒢¯\underline{\mathscr{G}}.

3.6. Global sections and restriction of generalised Kac–Moody algebras

We first give an elementary lemma. It is the analogue of Proposition 3.5 for genuine Lie algebras (as opposed to generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebras in tensor categories of perverse sheaves/mixed Hodge modules), which we repeat for convenience.

Lemma 3.7.

Let A≔F/IA\coloneqq F/I be an associative algebra described as the quotient of the free associative algebra FF on a set of generators EE modulo a two-sided ideal I⊆FI\subseteq F generated by a subspace V⊆FV\subseteq F. We let E¯\overline{E} be the image of EE in AA. We let 𝔤\mathfrak{g} be the Lie subalgebra of AA generated by E¯\overline{E}. We assume that V⊆FreeLie⁡(E)⊆FV\subseteq\operatorname{Free}_{\mathrm{Lie}}(E)\subseteq F. Then, there is a canonical isomorphism A≅𝐔⁡(𝔤)A\cong\UEA(\mathfrak{g}).

Proposition 3.8.

We let cl:π0​(ℳ)→M\mathrm{cl}\colon\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M})\rightarrow M be a morphism of monoids, where MM is a finitely generated, commutative and cancellative and set

  2. (2)

    The derived global sections H∗⁡(𝔫ℳ,(−,−),𝒢+)\HO^{*}(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},(-,-),\mathscr{G}}) is a Lie algebra, isomorphic to the positive part 𝔫M,(−,−),P+\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{M,(-,-),P} of the generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra 𝔤M,(−,−),P\mathfrak{g}_{M,(-,-),P}.

By the Künneth formula, H∗\HO^{*} is a monoidal functor. H∗⁡(𝐔⁡(𝔫ℳ,(−,−),𝒢+))=Free⁡(⨁m∈ΦM,(−,−)+H∗⁡(𝒢m))/H∗⁡(ℐℳ,𝒢,Alg)\HO^{*}(\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M},(-,-),\mathscr{G}}))=\operatorname{Free}\left(\bigoplus_{m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}}\HO^{*}(\mathscr{G}_{m})\right)/\HO^{*}(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{M},\mathscr{G},\mathrm{Alg}})

and H∗⁡(ℐℳ,𝒢,Alg)\HO^{*}(\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{M},\mathscr{G},\mathrm{Alg}}) is the two-sided ideal of Free⁡(⨁m∈ΦM,(−,−)+H∗⁡(𝒢m))\operatorname{Free}\left(\bigoplus_{m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}}\HO^{*}(\mathscr{G}_{m})\right) generated by H∗⁡(ℛm,n)\HO^{*}(\mathscr{R}_{m,n}) for m,n∈ΦM,(−,−)+m,n\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}. This proves (1). Since Rm,n⊆FreeLie⁡(⨁m∈ΦM,(−,−)+H∗⁡(𝒢m))R_{m,n}\subseteq\operatorname{Free}_{\mathrm{Lie}}(\bigoplus_{m\in\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}}\HO^{*}(\mathscr{G}_{m})), (2) follows thanks to Lemma 3.7. ∎
