4. Moduli stacks of objects in 22-dimensional categories

We recall the categorical and geometric framework of [DHS22].

4.1. Moduli stacks of objects

We let 𝒞\mathscr{C} be a 𝐂\mathbf{C}-linear dg-category, and let 𝕸⊆𝕸𝒞\bm{\mathfrak{M}}\subseteq\bm{\mathfrak{M}}_{\mathscr{C}} be a 11-Artin open substack of the stack of objects of 𝒞\mathscr{C} (in the sense of [TV07]). We denote by 𝔐=t0​(𝕸)\mathfrak{M}=t_{0}(\bm{\mathfrak{M}}) its classical truncation. We assume that 𝔐\mathfrak{M} parametrises objects of an admissible (in the sense of [Bei+18, §1.2]) finite length Abelian subcategory 𝒜\mathcal{A} of the homotopy category H0⁡(𝒞)\HO^{0}(\mathscr{C}). For X=Spec⁡(A)X=\operatorname{Spec}(A), XX-points of 𝕸𝒞\bm{\mathfrak{M}}_{\mathscr{C}} correspond to pseudo-perfect 𝒞⊗𝐂A\mathscr{C}\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}A-modules NN, i.e. bimodules NN that are perfect as AA-modules. Given a pair of such modules we obtain the dg AA-module RHom𝒞⊗𝐂A⁡(N,N′)\operatorname{RHom}_{\mathscr{C}\otimes_{\mathbf{C}}A}(N,N^{\prime}). This defines the RHom complex on 𝕸𝒞×2\bm{\mathfrak{M}}_{\mathscr{C}}^{\times 2}. We define the RHom\operatorname{RHom} complex on 𝔐×2\mathfrak{M}^{\times 2} by restriction.

4.2. Globally presented quasi-smooth morphisms

In this section we recall some terminology from [DHS22, §4] that we use in §4.3. We let 𝒞∙\mathcal{C}^{\bullet} be a graded perfect complex on a 1-Artin derived stack 𝕸\bm{\mathfrak{M}} with 𝒞i=0\mathcal{C}^{i}=0 for i⩾2i\geqslant 2. Let Q∈Der𝕸⁡(Tot𝕸⁡(𝒞∙))Q\in\operatorname{Der}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}(\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet})) be a degree one derivation that vanishes on the zero section, and satisfies [Q,Q]=0[Q,Q]=0.

Associated to this data is the derived 𝕸\bm{\mathfrak{M}}-stack Tot𝕸Q⁡(𝒞∙)\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}^{Q}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet}), which is the total space construction Tot𝕸⁡(𝒞∙)\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet}), with the differential twisted by QQ. For a precise definition of Tot𝕸Q⁡(𝒞∙)\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}^{Q}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet}) see [DHS22, §4.3]. We denote the projection

(4.1) 𝝅:Tot𝕸Q⁡(𝒞∙)⟶𝕸.\bm{\pi}\colon\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}^{Q}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet})\longrightarrow\bm{\mathfrak{M}}.

We call a morphism of the form (4.1) a globally presented quasi-smooth morphism. A global presentation of a quasi-smooth morphism of derived stacks 𝒇:𝖃→𝖄\bm{f}\colon\bm{\mathfrak{X}}\to\bm{\mathfrak{Y}} is a commutative diagram of 1-Artin stacks

where the vertical morphisms are equivalences and the bottom morphism is a globally presented quasi-smooth morphism.

Let (𝒞∙,Q𝒞)(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet},Q_{\mathcal{C}}) and (𝒞′⁣∙,Q𝒞′)(\mathcal{C}^{\prime\bullet},Q_{\mathcal{C}^{\prime}}) be global presentations of quasi-smooth morphisms, with both 𝒞∙\mathcal{C}^{\bullet} and 𝒞′⁣∙\mathcal{C}^{\prime\bullet} graded vector bundles over the same stack 𝕸\bm{\mathfrak{M}}. Let 𝒇:Tot𝕸⁡(𝒞∙)→Tot𝕸⁡(𝒞′⁣∙)\bm{f}\colon\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet})\rightarrow\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime\bullet}) be a morphism over 𝕸\bm{\mathfrak{M}} such that Q𝒞=𝒇∗​Q𝒞′Q_{\mathcal{C}}=\bm{f}^{*}Q_{\mathcal{C}^{\prime}}, and such that the induced morphism of complexes ((𝒞∙)∨,d𝒞)→((𝒞′⁣∙)∨,d𝒞′)((\mathcal{C}^{\bullet})^{\vee},d_{\mathcal{C}})\rightarrow((\mathcal{C}^{\prime\bullet})^{\vee},d_{\mathcal{C}^{\prime}}) is a quasi-isomorphism, inducing an equivalence Tot𝕸Q𝒞⁡(𝒞∙)→Tot𝕸Q𝒞′⁡(𝒞′⁣∙).\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}^{Q_{\mathcal{C}}}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet})\rightarrow\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}^{Q_{\mathcal{C}^{\prime}}}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime\bullet}). We call an equivalence defined via such an 𝒇\bm{f} a global equivalence.

Globally presented morphisms over a fixed stack 𝕸\bm{\mathfrak{M}} are closed under composition: if Tot𝕹Q′⁡(𝒞′)→𝕹\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{N}}}^{Q^{\prime}}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime})\to\bm{\mathfrak{N}} and 𝕹≃Tot𝕸Q⁡(𝒞)→𝕸\bm{\mathfrak{N}}\simeq\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}^{Q}(\mathcal{C})\to\bm{\mathfrak{M}} are globally presented quasi-smooth morphisms, then the composition 𝝅∘𝝅′\bm{\pi}\circ\bm{\pi}^{\prime} is globally presented by Tot𝕸Q+Q′⁡(𝒞⊕𝒞′~)→𝕸\operatorname{Tot}^{Q+Q^{\prime}}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}(\mathcal{C}\oplus\widetilde{\mathcal{C}^{\prime}})\to\bm{\mathfrak{M}}, where 𝒞′~\widetilde{\mathcal{C}^{\prime}} is a graded perfect complex on 𝕸\bm{\mathfrak{M}}. We define the 2-category 𝙶𝙿𝚛𝚎𝚜𝕸\GPres_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}} to be the 2-category having as objects the global presentations Tot𝕸Q⁡(𝒞∙)→𝕸\operatorname{Tot}_{\bm{\mathfrak{M}}}^{Q}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet})\rightarrow\bm{\mathfrak{M}}, 1-morphisms given by projections of globally presented quasi-smooth 𝕸\bm{\mathfrak{M}}-stacks, and 2-morphisms defined by global equivalences.

4.3. Assumptions on the stack of objects

For the construction of relative CoHAs in [DHS22], various assumptions are made on the stack of objects in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which we now recall. In concrete applications they are all known to hold; see [DHS22] for a more thorough treatment of these, as well as the assumptions 4–6 that follow. The first three concern the stack of objects 𝔐\mathfrak{M} from §4.1. Assumptions 1–3 are necessary for the construction of the CoHA product. Assumptions 4 and 6 allow us to use the neighbourhood theorem of [Dav21]. Assumption 5 is used to defined the BPS algebra.

Assumption 1 (Assumption for the construction of the pushforward by pp).

Let 𝔈​𝔵​𝔞​𝔠​𝔱\mathfrak{Exact} be the (classical truncation of the) stack of short exact sequences in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. We let p:𝔈​𝔵​𝔞​𝔠​𝔱→𝔐p\colon\mathfrak{Exact}\rightarrow\mathfrak{M} be the morphism forgetting the extreme terms of the short exact sequence. We assume that pp is a proper and representable morphism of stacks.

Let ℋ∙\mathcal{H}^{\bullet} be the RHom complex on 𝔐×𝔐\mathfrak{M}\times\mathfrak{M} (§4.1), and set 𝒞∙=ℋ∙​[1]\mathcal{C}^{\bullet}=\mathcal{H}^{\bullet}[1]. The stack 𝕰=Tot𝔐×𝔐⁡(𝒞∙)\bm{\mathfrak{E}}=\operatorname{Tot}_{\mathfrak{M}\times\mathfrak{M}}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet}) carries a universal bundle of (shifted) homomorphisms of objects in 𝒞\mathscr{C}, so that we have a natural identification t0​(𝕰)=𝔈​𝔵​𝔞​𝔠​𝔱t_{0}(\bm{\mathfrak{E}})=\mathfrak{Exact}, and a morphism 𝒑:𝕰→𝔐\bm{p}\colon\bm{\mathfrak{E}}\rightarrow\mathfrak{M} given by sending the morphism f:ρ→ρ′f\colon\rho\rightarrow\rho^{\prime} to cone​(f)​[1]\mathrm{cone}(f)[1]. Then p=t0​(𝒑)p=t_{0}(\bm{p}) is the morphism sending a short exact sequence to its middle term.

Assumption 2 (Assumption for the construction of the virtual pullback by 𝒒\bm{q}).

We assume that 𝔐\mathfrak{M} has the resolution property, i.e. every coherent sheaf on 𝔐\mathfrak{M} is a quotient of a vector bundle. For all ℳa,ℳb∈π0​(ℳ)\mathcal{M}_{a},\mathcal{M}_{b}\in\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}) we assume that the morphism 𝐪a,b:Tot𝔐a×𝔐b⁡(𝒞a,b∙)→𝔐a×𝔐b\bm{q}_{a,b}\colon\operatorname{Tot}_{\mathfrak{M}_{a}\times\mathfrak{M}_{b}}(\mathcal{C}^{\bullet}_{a,b})\rightarrow\mathfrak{M}_{a}\times\mathfrak{M}_{b} is represented by a globally presented quasi-smooth morphism 𝐪a,b′\bm{q}^{\prime}_{a,b}.

We note that, for the second part of Assumption 2 to be satisfied, it is enough for the RHom complex to be globally presented by a three-term complex of vector bundles, which is generally easy to check in examples. There are general criteria ensuring the resolution property [Tot04, Gro17].

Assumption 3 (Assumption for associativity).

We assume that the stack 𝔉​𝔦​𝔩​𝔱\mathfrak{Filt} of three step filtrations has a derived enhancement 𝕱​𝐢​𝐥​𝐭\bm{\mathfrak{F}ilt} which is globally presented over 𝔐×𝔐×𝔐\mathfrak{M}\times\mathfrak{M}\times\mathfrak{M} and and compatibly globally presented over 𝔐×𝕰\mathfrak{M}\times\bm{\mathfrak{E}} and 𝕰×𝔐\bm{\mathfrak{E}}\times\mathfrak{M}. More precisely, consider the diagram of derived stacks

Then we assume that (4.2) is represented by a diagram of globally presented quasi-smooth morphisms (i.e., a diagram in 𝙶𝙿𝚛𝚎𝚜\GPres) and we assume that the global presentations in this diagram are globally equivalent to the natural pullbacks of 𝐪′\bm{q}^{\prime}. For a completely precise formulation of this assumption see [DHS22, Assumption 3].

4.4. Assumptions on the good moduli space

The construction of the BPS algebra in §6.2 requires the existence of a good moduli space, satisfying various extra assumptions. Again, in concrete applications, they are all well-known to hold; see [DHS22] for a leisurely discussion.

Assumption 4.

The stack 𝔐\mathfrak{M} has a good moduli space 𝔐→𝙹𝙷ℳ\mathfrak{M}\xrightarrow{\JH}\mathcal{M} in the sense of [Alp13], and ℳ\mathcal{M} is a scheme.

The scheme ℳ\mathcal{M} is endowed with a monoid structure given by the direct sum:

⊕:ℳ×ℳ\displaystyle\oplus\colon\mathcal{M}\times\mathcal{M} ⟶ℳ\displaystyle\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}
(x,y)\displaystyle(x,y) ⟼x⊕y\displaystyle\longmapsto x\oplus y

obtained from the direct sum ⊕:𝔐×𝔐→𝔐\oplus\colon\mathfrak{M}\times\mathfrak{M}\rightarrow\mathfrak{M} and universality of the good moduli space 𝙹𝙷:𝔐→ℳ\JH\colon\mathfrak{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}. Note that the following diagram commutes:

If ℳa\mathcal{M}_{a} is a connected component of ℳ\mathcal{M}, we define 𝔐a≔𝙹𝙷−1⁡(ℳa)\mathfrak{M}_{a}\coloneqq\JH^{-1}(\mathcal{M}_{a}), and for a∈K⁡(𝒜)a\in\K(\mathcal{A}), where cl:π0​(ℳ)→K⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{cl}\colon\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M})\rightarrow\K(\mathcal{A}) is a morphism of monoids, we define 𝔐a\mathfrak{M}_{a} similarly (thus 𝔐a=⨆a′∈cl−1​(a)𝔐a′\mathfrak{M}_{a}=\bigsqcup_{a^{\prime}\in\mathrm{cl}^{-1}(a)}\mathfrak{M}_{a^{\prime}}).

Assumption 5.

We assume that the morphism ⊕\oplus is finite.

Given that the morphism ⊕\oplus is easily seen to be quasi-finite, this amounts to requesting that ⊕\oplus is a proper morphism.

To apply the local neighbourhood theorem (Theorem 4.2) on closed points of the moduli stacks 𝔐\mathfrak{M} we make the following additional Assumption 6.

Assumption 6.

Suppose we are in the situation of §4.1 and Assumptions 4 and 5 are satisfied. Given a collection of points x1,…,xr∈ℳx_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\in\mathcal{M} parametrising simple objects ℱ¯={ℱ1,…,ℱr}\underline{\mathcal{F}}=\{\mathcal{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{F}_{r}\} of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, the full dg subcategory of 𝒞\mathscr{C} containing ℱ¯\underline{\mathcal{F}} carries a right 2-Calabi–Yau (2CY) structure in the sense of [BD19, §3.1].

Again, this somewhat technical assumption is known to hold in examples we encounter, since by [BD19, Theorem 3.1], the existence of the required right 2CY structure will follow from the existence of a left 2CY structure on the category 𝒞\mathscr{C}, which is constructed in the examples appearing in this paper in [loc. cit.].

Making these rather general assumptions, we have the following theorem. The 2CY assumption (Assumption 6) then plays a crucial role in the definition of the BPS algebra appearing in §6.2.

Theorem 4.1 ([DHS22, §9]).

Under Assumptions 1-5 there is a virtual pullback along 𝐪a,b′\bm{q}^{\prime}_{a,b} and a push-forward along pp, yielding the cohomological Hall algebra product

(4.3) 𝔪:𝙹𝙷∗𝔻𝐐¯𝔐vir⊡𝙹𝙷∗𝔻𝐐¯𝔐vir≔⊕∗(𝙹𝙷×𝙹𝙷)∗𝔻𝐐¯𝔐×𝔐vir⟶𝙹𝙷∗𝔻𝐐¯𝔐vir\mathfrak{m}\colon\JH_{*}\mathbb{D}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}}^{\mathrm{vir}}\boxdot\JH_{*}\mathbb{D}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}}^{\mathrm{vir}}\coloneqq\oplus_{*}(\JH\times\JH)_{*}\mathbb{D}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}^{\mathrm{vir}}_{\mathfrak{M}\times\mathfrak{M}}\longrightarrow\JH_{*}\mathbb{D}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}}^{\mathrm{vir}}

which endows the mixed Hodge module complex 𝙹𝙷∗⁡𝔻​𝐐¯𝔐vir\JH_{*}\mathbb{D}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}}^{\mathrm{vir}} with the structure of an associative algebra in the symmetric monoidal category (𝒟+​(MHM​(ℳ)),⊡)(\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M})),\boxdot).

4.5. Serre subcategories

Let 𝔐→𝙹𝙷ℳ\mathfrak{M}\xrightarrow{\JH}\mathcal{M} be as in Assumption 4 a good moduli space for the stack of objects 𝔐\mathfrak{M} as in §4.1. Fix a locally closed submonoid ℳ′⊆ℳ\mathcal{M}^{\prime}\subseteq\mathcal{M} that is stable under direct summands, i.e. saturated (if x⊕y∈ℳ′x\oplus y\in\mathcal{M}^{\prime}, then x,y∈ℳ′x,y\in\mathcal{M}^{\prime}). We define ℬ\mathcal{B} to be the full Abelian subcategory of 𝒜\mathcal{A} generated by the objects represented by the closed points of ℳ′\mathcal{M}^{\prime} under taking extensions. Typically, ℬ\mathcal{B} will be defined to be the full subcategory of objects of 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfying some support or nilpotency condition. Since ℳ\mathcal{M} parametrises semisimple objects in 𝒜\mathcal{A}, ℬ\mathcal{B} is a Serre subcategory (an Abelian subcategory stable under extensions, subobjects and quotients).

Let ℬ\mathcal{B} be a Serre subcategory of 𝒜\mathcal{A} corresponding to a locally closed submonoid ℳℬ⊆ℳ\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}}\subseteq\mathcal{M}. We define 𝔐ℬ⊆𝔐\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{B}}\subseteq\mathfrak{M} to be the substack parametrising objects of ℬ\mathcal{B}, which we define via the following Cartesian square

The morphism 𝔐ℬ→ℳℬ\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{B}}\to\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}} is a good moduli space by [Alp13, Proposition 4.7 (i)]. Let π0​(ℳℬ)\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}}) be the monoid of connected components of ℳℬ\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}}. The monoid structure ⊕:π0​(ℳℬ)×π0​(ℳℬ)→π0​(ℳℬ)\oplus:\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}})\times\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}})\rightarrow\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}}) is induced by the direct sum. We choose a monoid K⁡(ℬ)\K(\mathcal{B}) and a surjective morphism of monoids cl:π0​(ℳℬ)→K⁡(ℬ)\mathrm{cl}\colon\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}})\rightarrow\K(\mathcal{B}) with finite fibres, where the target is a monoid for which the morphism K⁡(ℬ)→K⁡(ℬ)^\K(\mathcal{B})\rightarrow\widehat{\K(\mathcal{B})} is an inclusion in a lattice.

The monoid of connected components of the stack 𝔐ℬ\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{B}} coincides with π0​(ℳℬ)\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}}), since the fibres of 𝙹𝙷\JH are connected, by [Alp13, Theorem 4.16 (vii)]. For a∈K⁡(ℬ)a\in\K(\mathcal{B}), we denote by 𝔐ℬ,a\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{B},a} and ℳℬ,a\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B},a} the corresponding (finite) unions of connected components.

For any object ℱ\mathcal{F} of ℬ\mathcal{B} (resp. 𝐂\mathbf{C}-point xx of 𝔐ℬ\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{B}} or ℳℬ\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}}), we let [ℱ][\mathcal{F}] (resp. [x][x]) be cl\mathrm{cl} applied to the connected component of xx. We will refer to [x][x] as the class of xx. The Euler form automatically factors through π0​(ℳℬ)\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}}) to define a bilinear form:

(−,−)𝒞:π0​(ℳℬ)×π0​(ℳℬ)⟶𝐙.(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}}\colon\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}})\times\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}})\longrightarrow\mathbf{Z}.

We assume that it moreover factors through cl\mathrm{cl}. The pair (K⁡(ℬ),(−,−)𝒞)(\K(\mathcal{B}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}}) will provide the combinatorial input required in §3.1.

4.6. The local neighbourhood theorem

Let 𝒞\mathscr{C}, 𝔐\mathfrak{M} and ℳ\mathcal{M} be as above, satisfying Assumptions 4 and 6. Then the closed points of ℳ\mathcal{M} are in bijection with semisimple objects of the category 𝒜\mathcal{A} and the map 𝙹𝙷\JH sends a 𝐂\mathbf{C}-point of 𝔐\mathfrak{M} corresponding to an object ℱ\mathcal{F} of 𝒜\mathcal{A} to the 𝐂\mathbf{C}-point of ℳ\mathcal{M} corresponding to the associated graded object of ℱ\mathcal{F} with respect to some Jordan–Hölder filtration.

4.6.1. Σ\Sigma-collections

Let ℱ\mathcal{F} be an object in a 𝐂\mathbf{C}-linear Abelian category 𝒜\mathcal{A}, which we will assume is realised as a subcategory of the homotopy category of some dg category 𝒞\mathscr{C}. We say that ℱ\mathcal{F} is a Σ\Sigma-object if Ext𝒞∗⁡(ℱ,ℱ)≅H∗⁡(S,𝐂)\operatorname{Ext}^{*}_{\mathscr{C}}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{F})\cong\HO^{*}(S,\mathbf{C}) for SS a closed Riemann surface (of some genus g⩾0g\geqslant 0). If ℱ¯={ℱ1,…,ℱr}\underline{\mathcal{F}}=\{\mathcal{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{F}_{r}\} is a collection of objects of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we say that ℱ¯\underline{\mathcal{F}} is a Σ\Sigma-collection if each ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} is a Σ\Sigma-object and for m≠nm\neq n, Hom⁡(ℱm,ℱn)=0\operatorname{Hom}(\mathcal{F}_{m},\mathcal{F}_{n})=0.

Let ℱ¯={ℱ1,…,ℱr}\underline{\mathcal{F}}=\{\mathcal{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{F}_{r}\} be a Σ\Sigma-collection of objects of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. We define the Ext-quiver of ℱ¯\underline{\mathcal{F}} as the quiver Q¯ℱ¯\overline{Q}_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}} having as set of vertices ℱ¯\underline{\mathcal{F}}, and having ext1⁡(ℱi,ℱj)\operatorname{ext}^{1}(\mathcal{F}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{j}) arrows from ii to jj. When ext1⁡(ℱi,ℱj)=ext1⁡(ℱj,ℱi)\operatorname{ext}^{1}(\mathcal{F}_{i},\mathcal{F}_{j})=\operatorname{ext}^{1}(\mathcal{F}_{j},\mathcal{F}_{i}) for any 1⩽i,j⩽r1\leqslant i,j\leqslant r and this number is even if i=ji=j, then Q¯ℱ¯\overline{Q}_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}} is the double of some (usually non-unique) quiver Qℱ¯Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}. This condition is for example satisfied for right 22-Calabi–Yau categories as in §4.1. Accordingly, we make Assumption 6. We will refer to Qℱ¯Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}} as a half of the Ext-quiver of ℱ¯\underline{\mathcal{F}}.

We have a morphism of monoids

λℱ¯:𝐍ℱ¯⟶K⁡(𝒜)𝐦⟼∑i=1rmi​[ℱi].\begin{split}\lambda_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}\colon\mathbf{N}^{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}&\longrightarrow\K(\mathcal{A})\\ \mathbf{m}&\longmapsto\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}[\mathcal{F}_{i}].\end{split}

We also have a morphism of monoids

(4.4) ıℱ¯:𝐍ℱ¯⟶ℳ\imath_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}\colon\mathbf{N}^{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}\longrightarrow\mathcal{M}

mapping 𝐦∈𝐍ℱ¯\mathbf{m}\in\mathbf{N}^{\underline{\mathcal{F}}} to the point of ℳ\mathcal{M} corresponding to the object ⨁i=1rℱi⊕mi\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\oplus m_{i}}, i.e. 1ℱi↦xi1_{\mathcal{F}_{i}}\mapsto x_{i} if we denote by xi∈ℳx_{i}\in\mathcal{M} the point corresponding to ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i}.

If x∈ℳ𝒜x\in\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}, it corresponds to a semisimple object ℱ=⨁i=1rℱi⊕di\mathcal{F}=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\oplus d_{i}}. We define (Qx,𝐝x)(Q_{x},\mathbf{d}_{x}) to be the pair formed by a half of the Ext-quiver of ℱ¯≔{ℱ1,…,ℱr}\underline{\mathcal{F}}\coloneqq\{\mathcal{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{F}_{r}\} and the dimension vector 𝐝x=(d1,…,dr)\mathbf{d}_{x}=(d_{1},\ldots,d_{r}). 4.6.2. The local neighbourhood theorem

We recall here the local neighbourhood theorem for 22-Calabi–Yau categories [Dav21, Theorem 5.11], which we will use in the next section to investigate the geometry of components of moduli spaces corresponding to roots for general 2CY categories.

Theorem 4.2.

Let 𝙹𝙷:𝔐→ℳ\JH\colon\mathfrak{M}\rightarrow\mathcal{M} be a good moduli space, locally of finite type with reductive stabilizer groups. We assume that 𝔐=t0​(𝕸)\mathfrak{M}=t_{0}(\bm{\mathfrak{M}}) is an Artin stack, where 𝕸⊆𝕸𝒞\bm{\mathfrak{M}}\subseteq\bm{\mathfrak{M}}_{\mathscr{C}} is an open substack of the stack of objects of a dg-category 𝒞\mathscr{C}. Let xx be a closed 𝐂\mathbf{C}-valued point of 𝔐\mathfrak{M} corresponding to an object ℱ=⨁1⩽i⩽rℱi⊕mi\mathcal{F}=\bigoplus_{1\leqslant i\leqslant r}\mathcal{F}_{i}^{\oplus m_{i}} and assume that the full dg-subcategory of 𝒞\mathscr{C} containing ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i}, 1⩽i⩽r1\leqslant i\leqslant r carries a right 2CY structure and ℱ¯={ℱi}1⩽i⩽r\underline{\mathcal{F}}=\{\mathcal{F}_{i}\}_{1\leqslant i\leqslant r} is a Σ\Sigma-collection. We let QQ be a half of the Ext-quiver of the collection ℱ¯={ℱi:1⩽i⩽r}\underline{\mathcal{F}}=\{\mathcal{F}_{i}:1\leqslant i\leqslant r\}. Then, there is a pointed affine GL𝐦\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbf{m}}-variety (H,y)(H,y), and an analytic neighbourhood U⊆HU\subseteq H of yy such that if 𝒰x\mathcal{U}_{x} (resp. 𝔘x\mathfrak{U}_{x}) denotes the image of UU by the canonical map H→H//GL𝐦H\rightarrow H/\!\!/\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbf{m}} (resp. H→H/GL𝐦H\rightarrow H/\mathrm{GL}_{\mathbf{m}}), there is a commutative diagram

in which the horizontal morphisms are analytic open immersions and the two squares are Cartesian.

The original version of this theorem gives an étale local description of the map (𝔐,x)→(ℳ,𝙹𝙷⁡(x))(\mathfrak{M},x)\rightarrow(\mathcal{M},\JH(x)). For applications to calculating perverse sheaves (as opposed to objects in the derived category of perverse sheaves), working in the analytic topology has some advantages. Under the assumptions given in §4.6, the theorem applies for any 𝐂\mathbf{C}-valued closed point xx of 𝔐\mathfrak{M}.

5. Roots and the geometry of the good moduli space

5.1. Roots for preprojective algebras

Let QQ be a quiver and let ΠQ\Pi_{Q} be its preprojective algebra. We let (−,−)𝒢2​(𝐂​Q):𝐍Q0×𝐍Q0→𝐙(-,-)_{\mathscr{G}_{2}(\mathbf{C}Q)}\colon\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}\times\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Z} be the Euler form of the derived preprojective algebra 𝒢2​(𝐂​Q)\mathscr{G}_{2}(\mathbf{C}Q). It is the symmetrization of the Euler form of QQ and, when QQ is not Dynkin, it coincides with the Euler form of ΠQ\Pi_{Q} itself. We let

ΣΠQ≔{𝐝∈𝐍Q0∖{0}∣ for any nontrivial decomposition 𝐝=∑j=1r𝐝j,𝐝j∈𝐍Q0∖{0} one has (2−(𝐝,𝐝)𝒢2​(𝐂​Q))>∑j=1r(2−(𝐝j,𝐝j)𝒢2​(𝐂​Q))}.\Sigma_{\Pi_{Q}}\coloneqq\left\{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}\smallsetminus\{0\}\mid\text{ for any nontrivial decomposition }\mathbf{d}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\mathbf{d}_{j},\mathbf{d}_{j}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}\smallsetminus\{0\}\right.\\ \left.\text{ one has }(2-(\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d})_{\mathscr{G}_{2}(\mathbf{C}Q)})>\sum_{j=1}^{r}(2-(\mathbf{d}_{j},\mathbf{d}_{j})_{\mathscr{G}_{2}(\mathbf{C}Q)})\right\}.

We let Q0Q_{0} be the set of real vertices (loop-free vertices of QQ). For i∈Q0i\in Q_{0}, we have a reflection

si:𝐙Q0→𝐙Q0𝐝↦𝐝−(1i,𝐝)𝒢2​(𝐂​Q)​1i.\begin{matrix}s_{i}&\colon&\mathbf{Z}^{Q_{0}}&\rightarrow&\mathbf{Z}^{Q_{0}}\\ &&\mathbf{d}&\mapsto&\mathbf{d}-(1_{i},\mathbf{d})_{\mathscr{G}_{2}(\mathbf{C}Q)}1_{i}.\end{matrix}

These reflections generate the Weyl group WQW_{Q} of QQ.

The fundamental cone is

CΠQ≔{𝐝∈𝐍Q0∖{0}∣supp⁡(𝐝)​ is connected and ​(𝐝,1i)𝒢2​(𝐂​Q)⩽0​ for every i∈Q0},C_{\Pi_{Q}}\coloneqq\{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}\smallsetminus\{0\}\mid\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf{d})\text{ is connected and }(\mathbf{d},1_{i})_{\mathscr{G}_{2}(\mathbf{C}Q)}\leqslant 0\text{ for every $i\in Q_{0}$}\},

where the support supp⁡(𝐝)\operatorname{supp}(\mathbf{d}) of the dimension vector 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} is defined as the full subquiver containing the vertices i∈Q0i\in Q_{0} such that di≠0d_{i}\neq 0. In the definition of the fundamental cone, one can replace Q0Q_{0} by Q0Q_{0} since if ii is a vertex with at least one loop, (1i,𝐝)⩽0(1_{i},\mathbf{d})\leqslant 0 automatically for any 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}. We embed Q0Q_{0} inside 𝐍Q0\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} by sending i↦1ii\mapsto 1_{i}. Following [Cra01], we let

RΠQ≔WQ⋅Q0∪(±WQ⋅CΠQ)R_{\Pi_{Q}}\coloneqq W_{Q}\cdot Q_{0}\cup(\pm W_{Q}\cdot C_{\Pi_{Q}})

be the set of roots of the quiver QQ. We let RΠQ+≔RΠQ∩𝐍Q0R_{\Pi_{Q}}^{+}\coloneqq R_{\Pi_{Q}}\cap\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} be the set of positive roots. As in [loc. cit] we define the set

Σ′ΠQ≔{𝐝∈RΠQ+∣ for any nontrivial decomposition 𝐝=∑j=1r𝐝j,𝐝j∈RΠQ+∖{0} one has (2−(𝐝,𝐝)𝒢2​(𝐂​Q))>∑j=1r(2−(𝐝j,𝐝j)𝒢2​(𝐂​Q))}.\Sigma^{\prime}_{\Pi_{Q}}\coloneqq\left\{\mathbf{d}\in R_{\Pi_{Q}}^{+}\mid\text{ for any nontrivial decomposition }\mathbf{d}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\mathbf{d}_{j},\mathbf{d}_{j}\in R_{\Pi_{Q}}^{+}\smallsetminus\{0\}\right.\\ \left.\text{ one has }(2-(\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d})_{\mathscr{G}_{2}(\mathbf{C}Q)})>\sum_{j=1}^{r}(2-(\mathbf{d}_{j},\mathbf{d}_{j})_{\mathscr{G}_{2}(\mathbf{C}Q)})\right\}.

6. The cohomological Hall algebra and the BPS algebra

We let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a 22-Calabi–Yau Abelian category, and 𝙹𝙷:𝔐𝒜→ℳ𝒜\JH\colon\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} be its moduli stack of objects and good moduli space as in §4.

6.1. The cohomological Hall algebra

In [DHS22, §9], we define the relative cohomological Hall algebra of 𝒜\mathcal{A} as an algebra structure on the complex of mixed Hodge modules 𝒜¯𝒜≔(𝙹𝙷𝒜)∗​𝔻​𝐐¯𝔐𝒜vir\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\coloneqq(\JH_{\mathcal{A}})_{*}\mathbb{D}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}}^{\mathrm{vir}}, given by the morphism (c.f. (4.3))

𝔪:𝒜¯𝒜⊡𝒜¯𝒜→𝒜¯𝒜\mathfrak{m}\colon\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\boxdot\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}

satisfying the standard axioms of associativity and unitality in monoidal categories, where the tensor structure ⊡\boxdot on 𝒟+​(MHM​(ℳ))\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M})) is defined as in §3.5. The product is defined via (virtual) pullback and pushforward from the stack of short exact sequences of objects in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. The mixed Hodge module 𝐐¯𝔐𝒜vir∈𝒟+​(MHM⁡(𝔐𝒜))\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}}^{\mathrm{vir}}\in\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}})) is the twisted constant mixed Hodge module 𝐐¯𝔐𝒜,a⊗𝐋(a,a)𝒞/2\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A},a}}\otimes\mathbf{L}^{(a,a)_{\mathscr{C}}/2} on the connected component 𝔐𝒜,a\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A},a} of 𝔐𝒜\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}. We are committing here a standard abuse of notation: while we do not define anywhere the derived category of mixed Hodge modules on the stack 𝔐𝒜\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}, the direct image (𝙹𝙷𝒜)∗​𝔻​𝐐¯𝔐𝒜vir(\JH_{\mathcal{A}})_{*}\mathbb{D}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}}^{\mathrm{vir}} is still defined, as an unbounded complex of mixed Hodge modules: see [Dav20, §2.1] for details.

The absolute cohomological Hall algebra is obtained by taking the derived global sections H∗⁡(𝒜¯𝒜)\HO^{*}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}), with the multiplication H∗⁡(𝔪)\HO^{*}(\mathfrak{m}). If ℬ⊆𝒜\mathcal{B}\subseteq\mathcal{A} is a Serre subcategory and ı:ℳℬ↪ℳ𝒜\imath\colon\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} is the inclusion of the submonoid parametrising semisimple objects of 𝒜\mathcal{A} contained in ℬ\mathcal{B}, we let 𝔐ℬ\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{B}} be the stack defined by the following Cartesian diagram:

Then, by base change, the morphism ı!𝔪\imath^{!}\mathfrak{m} gives ı!𝒜¯𝒜∈𝒟+(MHM(ℳℬ))\imath^{!}\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}})) an algebra structure. It is the relative cohomological Hall algebra of ℬ\mathcal{B}, and H∗(ı!𝒜¯𝒜)\HO^{*}(\imath^{!}\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}) is the absolute cohomological Hall algebra of ℬ\mathcal{B}. By base change in the diagram

which we implicitly assumed to be Cartesian (we say that ℳℬ\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}} is a saturated submonoid of ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}) the functor ı!:𝒟+(MHM(ℳ𝒜))→𝒟+(MHM(ℳℬ))\imath^{!}\colon\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}))\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{B}})) is strictly monoidal.

The cases most relevant to this paper are the following.

6.2. The BPS algebra

We let 𝒜\mathcal{A}, 𝙹𝙷𝒜:𝔐𝒜→ℳ𝒜\JH_{\mathcal{A}}\colon\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}, 𝒜¯𝒜=(𝙹𝙷𝒜)∗​𝔻​𝐐¯𝔐𝒜vir∈𝒟+​(MHM⁡(ℳ𝒜))\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}=(\JH_{\mathcal{A}})_{*}\mathbb{D}\underline{\mathbf{Q}}_{\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}}^{\mathrm{vir}}\in\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}})) and 𝔪:𝒜¯𝒜⊡𝒜¯𝒜→𝒜¯𝒜\mathfrak{m}\colon\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\boxdot\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}} be as in §4.1 and §6.1. In particular, we make assumptions 1–6.

Lemma 6.1.

The complex of mixed Hodge modules 𝒜¯𝒜\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}} is concentrated in nonnegative cohomological degrees: ℋi​(𝒜¯𝒜)=0\mathcal{H}^{i}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}})=0 for i<0i<0. The mixed Hodge module ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}) is semisimple.

Proof.

This is part of [Dav20, Theorem A], which shows, in particular, that the mixed Hodge module ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}) is pure of weight zero. ∎

It follows that τ⩽0​𝒜¯𝒜≅ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)\tau^{\leqslant 0}\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\cong\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}). Since ⊡\boxdot is bi-exact, it also follows that τ⩽0​(𝒜¯𝒜⊡𝒜¯𝒜)≅ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜⊡𝒜¯𝒜)≅ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)⊡ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)\tau^{\leqslant 0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\boxdot\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}})\cong\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\boxdot\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}})\cong\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}})\boxdot\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}).

Corollary 6.2.

The map ℋ0​(𝔪):ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)⊡ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)→ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathfrak{m})\colon\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}})\boxdot\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}})\rightarrow\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}) is an associative algebra in the monoidal category (MHM⁡(ℳ),⊡)(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}),\boxdot).

Proof.

This comes from the fact that 𝒜¯𝒜\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}} is concentrated in nonnegative cohomological degrees (Lemma 6.1). The operation ℋ0​(𝔪)\mathcal{H}^{0}(\mathfrak{m}) is associative because 𝔪\mathfrak{m} is. ∎

We set ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg:=ℋ0​(𝒜¯𝒜)\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}:=\mathcal{H}^{0}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}) with its algebra structure given above. This algebra object is called the relative BPS algebra. Its cohomology (derived global sections) is denoted BPS¯𝒜,Alg:=H∗⁡(ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg)\underline{\aBPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}:=\HO^{*}(\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}) and called the BPS algebra.

The next proposition follows from the decomposition theorem for 2CY categories [Dav21].

Proposition 6.3.

The natural morphism of algebras BPS¯𝒜,Alg→H∗⁡(𝒜¯𝒜)\underline{\aBPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}\rightarrow\HO^{*}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}) is injective.

Proof.

The decomposition theorem for 2CY categories of [Dav21, Theorem B] asserts in particular that the underlying complex of mixed Hodge modules 𝒜¯𝒜\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}} is the direct sum of its shifted cohomology mixed Hodge modules and so the map ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg→𝒜¯𝒜\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}} admits a retraction. Therefore, the map BPS¯𝒜,Alg→H∗⁡(𝒜¯𝒜)\underline{\mathrm{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}\rightarrow\HO^{*}(\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}) obtained by taking cohomology also admits a retraction and is injective. ∎

6.3. ψ\psi-twists

6.3.1. Twisted multiplication

In [DHS22], we introduce a twist of the multiplication of the cohomological Hall algebra by a bilinear form ψ\psi. This twist is necessary to have the structure of an enveloping algebra on the BPS algebra (it appears already in the PBW theorem for CoHAs of Jacobi algebras, see [DM20, §1.6]). In vague terms (made precise in [Hen22]), this twist exchanges the specialisation at q=−1q=-1 of the quantum group 𝐔q⁡(𝔤)\UEA_{q}(\mathfrak{g}) with the enveloping algebra 𝐔⁡(𝔤)\UEA(\mathfrak{g}) (the specialisation q=1q=1). In this section, we explain this twist.

As in §1.2 we choose a monoid K⁡(𝒜)\K(\mathcal{A}) and fix a morphism of monoids cl:π0​(ℳ𝒜)→K⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{cl}\colon\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}})\rightarrow\K(\mathcal{A}) through which the Euler form factors. We assume again that K⁡(𝒜)\K(\mathcal{A}) can be embedded in a lattice and that cl\mathrm{cl} has finite fibres. We let ψ:K⁡(𝒜)×K⁡(𝒜)→𝐙/2​𝐙\psi\colon\K(\mathcal{A})\times\K(\mathcal{A})\rightarrow\mathbf{Z}/2\mathbf{Z} be a bilinear form such that for any a,b∈K⁡(𝒜)a,b\in\K(\mathcal{A}),

ψ⁡(a,b)+ψ⁡(b,a)≡(a,b)𝒞(mod2).\psi(a,b)+\psi(b,a)\equiv(a,b)_{\mathscr{C}}\pmod{2}.

Such a bilinear form exists since for any a∈π0​(ℳ𝒜)a\in\pi_{0}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}), (a,a)𝒞≡0(mod2)(a,a)_{\mathscr{C}}\equiv 0\pmod{2}. Indeed, it follows that any matrix MM representing the form induced by (−,−)𝒞(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}} on K⁡(𝒜)\K(\mathcal{A}) has even entries on the diagonal, and we may define ψ⁡(−,−)\psi(-,-) via the matrix obtained by replacing all entries in MM above the diagonal by zeros.

For such a bilinear form ψ\psi, we let 𝒜¯𝒜ψ\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi} be the relative cohomological Hall algebra with the multiplication 𝔪a,bψ≔(−1)ψ⁡(a,b)​𝔪a,b:𝒜¯𝒜ψ⊠𝒜¯𝒜ψ→𝒜¯𝒜ψ\mathfrak{m}_{a,b}^{\psi}\coloneqq(-1)^{\psi(a,b)}\mathfrak{m}_{a,b}\colon\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi}\boxtimes\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi}. As complexes of mixed Hodge modules on ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}, 𝒜¯𝒜ψ=𝒜¯𝒜\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi}=\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}. The twisted multiplication induces twisted multiplications 𝔪ψ\mathfrak{m}^{\psi} on the relative BPS algebra ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}, on the absolute CoHA H∗⁡𝒜¯𝒜\HO^{*}\!\!\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}} and the absolute BPS algebra BPS¯𝒜,Alg\underline{\mathrm{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}. We denote by ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Algψ\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}, H∗⁡𝒜¯𝒜ψ\HO^{*}\!\!\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\psi} and BPS¯𝒜,Algψ\underline{\mathrm{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi} the algebra objects with the twisted multiplications.

6.3.2. Induced twist for Ext-quivers

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be an Abelian subcategory of a 2CY category as in §4. If ℱ¯\underline{\mathcal{F}} is a collection of simple objects of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, we have the Ext-quiver Q¯ℱ¯\overline{Q}_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}} (§4.6.1) and the preprojective algebra ΠQℱ¯\Pi_{Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}}. By Lemma 5.2, for any 𝐝,𝐝′∈𝐍(Qℱ¯)0\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{N}^{(Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}})_{0}}, ψ⁡(𝐝,𝐝′)+ψ⁡(𝐝′,𝐝)≡(𝐝,𝐝′)𝒢2​(𝐂​Qℱ¯)(mod2)\psi(\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d}^{\prime})+\psi(\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d})\equiv(\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d}^{\prime})_{\mathscr{G}_{2}(\mathbf{C}Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}})}\pmod{2}.

The relative cohomological Hall algebra 𝒜¯ΠQ(ψ)\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\Pi_{Q}}^{(\psi)}, the relative BPS algebra ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯ΠQ,Alg(ψ)\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Alg}}^{(\psi)} and the free algebra Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯ΠQ)\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\Pi_{Q}}) are 𝔾aL¯\mathbb{G}_{a}^{\overline{L}}-equivariant.

We adopt ideas from the proof of [DHS22]. Proposition 7.13.

The morphism Υ𝒜:Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯𝒜)→ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Algψ\Upsilon_{\mathcal{A}}\colon\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}})\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi} factors through Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯𝒜)→Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯𝒜)/ℐ¯𝒜,Alg\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}})\rightarrow\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}})/\underline{\mathcal{I}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}.

Step 1: Reduction to preprojective algebras of quivers

If there exists a simple mixed Hodge module ℱ¯⊆ℐ𝒜,Alg\underline{\mathscr{F}}\subseteq\mathcal{I}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}} such that the restriction of Υ𝒜\Upsilon_{\mathcal{A}} to ℱ¯\underline{\mathscr{F}} is non-zero, then we let xx be a point such that ıx!ℱ¯≠0\imath_{x}^{!}\underline{\mathscr{F}}\neq 0 where ıx:{x}→ℳ𝒜\imath_{x}\colon\{x\}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} is the inclusion [DHS22, Corollary 12.7]. We let ℱ¯={ℱ1,…​ℱr}\underline{\mathcal{F}}=\{\mathcal{F}_{1},\ldots\mathcal{F}_{r}\} be the corresponding collection of simple objects of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. We let ιℱ¯\iota_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}} be as in diagram (7.1). Then, ιℱ¯!Υ𝒜\iota_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}^{!}\Upsilon_{\mathcal{A}} does not vanish on ιℱ¯!ℱ¯\iota_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}^{!}\underline{\mathscr{F}}. But, by Proposition 7.7, if Qℱ¯Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}} is a quiver such that its double Qℱ¯¯\overline{Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}} is the Ext-quiver of ℱ¯={ℱ1,…,ℱr}\underline{\mathcal{F}}=\{\mathcal{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{F}_{r}\}, ι𝒩!ΥΠQℱ¯\iota_{\mathcal{N}}^{!}\Upsilon_{\Pi_{Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}}} does not vanish on ι𝒩!ℐ¯ΠQℱ¯,Alg\iota_{\mathcal{N}}^{!}\underline{\mathcal{I}}_{\Pi_{Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}},\mathrm{Alg}}. This implies that ΥΠQℱ¯\Upsilon_{\Pi_{Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}}} does not vanish on ℐ¯ΠQℱ¯,Alg\underline{\mathcal{I}}_{\Pi_{Q_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}},\mathrm{Alg}}. So if we can prove Proposition 7.13 for 𝒜=Rep⁡ΠQ\mathcal{A}=\operatorname{Rep}\Pi_{Q} for any quiver QQ, it is true for any Abelian category 𝒜\mathcal{A} satisfying the assumptions of §4.

Step 2: Proof for preprojective algebras of quivers We turn to the proof of Proposition 7.13 for 𝒜=Rep⁡(ΠQ)\mathcal{A}=\operatorname{Rep}(\Pi_{Q}).

We prove by induction the following claim.

By Propositions 7.5 and 7.7, both vertical arrows are isomorphisms. 7.7.3. The BPS Lie algebra

In §7.7.2, we proved Theorem 1.1, that is that we have an isomorphism in MHM⁡(ℳ𝒜)\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}})

ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Algψ≅𝐔⁡(𝔫ℳ𝒜,𝒢¯𝒜+)\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}\cong\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}},\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}}})

where 𝒢¯𝒜\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}} is as in §6.4.3, motivating the following definition:

Definition 7.15.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a 2-Calabi–Yau category satisfying our assumptions 1–6 in §4.3 and §4.4. The BPS Lie algebra sheaf of 𝒜\mathcal{A} is

ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie≔𝔫ℳ𝒜,𝒢¯𝒜+.\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}\coloneqq\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}},\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}}}.

In words, this is the generalised half Kac–Moody Lie algebra object in the tensor category of mixed Hodge modules on the coarse moduli space (as defined in §3.5), with generating mixed Hodge modules defined in §6.4.3. If ı△:ℳ𝒜△↪ℳ𝒜\imath_{\triangle}\colon\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} is the inclusion of a saturated monoid (in schemes) corresponding to a Serre subcategory, we define

𝔫¯𝒜△,+≔H∗(ı△!𝔫ℳ𝒜,𝒢¯𝒜+)\underline{\mathfrak{n}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle,+}\coloneqq\HO^{*}(\imath_{\triangle}^{!}\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}},\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}}})

and in particular 𝔫¯𝒜+≔H∗⁡(𝔫ℳ𝒜,𝒢¯𝒜)\underline{\mathfrak{n}}_{\mathcal{A}}^{+}\coloneqq\HO^{*}(\mathfrak{n}_{\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}},\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}}}). We denote by 𝔤𝒜△⊃𝔫𝒜△,+\mathfrak{g}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}}\supset\mathfrak{n}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle,+} the extension to the generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra as defined in Theorem 1.2.

7.8. Verdier duality and the compactly supported CoHA

Corollary 7.16.

The BPS algebra sheaf ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}} and the BPS Lie algebra sheaf ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}} are Verdier self-dual mixed Hodge modules on ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}. More precisely, each simple direct summand of ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}} (and hence of ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}) is Verdier self-dual.

Proof.

By Theorem 1.1, the relative BPS algebra is a quotient of Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯𝒜)\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}}) and so (by finiteness of ⊕\oplus which gives the commutation of ⊡\boxdot with Verdier duality), it suffices to prove the Verdier self-duality of each simple direct summand of Free⊡-Alg⁡(𝒢¯𝒜)\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sAlg}(\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}}). Such a simple direct summand appears in the pushforward of the ℐ​𝒞¯\underline{\mathcal{IC}} mixed Hodge module by the finite map ⊕′:∏i=1rℳ𝒜,mi×∏j=1sℳ𝒜,nj→ℳ𝒜\oplus^{\prime}\colon\prod_{i=1}^{r}\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m_{i}}\times\prod_{j=1}^{s}\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},n_{j}}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}, ((xi)1⩽i⩽r,(yj)1⩽j⩽s)↦⨁i=1rxili⊕⨁j=1syj((x_{i})_{1\leqslant i\leqslant r},(y_{j})_{1\leqslant j\leqslant s})\mapsto\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}x_{i}^{l_{i}}\oplus\bigoplus_{j=1}^{s}y_{j}, where mi∈ΣK⁡(𝒜)∩ΦK⁡(𝒜)+,isom_{i}\in\Sigma_{\K(\mathcal{A})}\cap\Phi^{+,\mathrm{iso}}_{\K(\mathcal{A})}, nj∈ΣK⁡(𝒜)∖(ΣK⁡(𝒜)∩ΦK⁡(𝒜)+,iso)n_{j}\in\Sigma_{\K(\mathcal{A})}\smallsetminus(\Sigma_{\K(\mathcal{A})}\cap\Phi^{+,\mathrm{iso}}_{\K(\mathcal{A})}) and li∈𝐙⩾1l_{i}\in\mathbf{Z}_{\geqslant 1}. The map ⊕′\oplus^{\prime} is small and is a covering over an open subspace of its image with structure group a product of symmetric groups. The corollary then follows from the fact that all representations of symmetric groups are self-dual. ∎

Recall the class map cl:ℳ𝒜→K⁡(𝒜)\mathrm{cl}\colon\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\K(\mathcal{A}) (§6.3.1). The absolute CoHA can be seen as cl∗​𝒜¯𝒜∈𝒟+​(MHM⁡(K⁡(𝒜)))\mathrm{cl}_{*}\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\K(\mathcal{A}))) endowed with the multiplication cl∗​𝔪\mathrm{cl}_{*}\mathfrak{m}. We also consider the variant using the functor cl!\mathrm{cl}_{!}. By the properness of ⊕\oplus (implying ⊕∗=⊕!\oplus_{*}=\oplus_{!}), cl!\mathrm{cl}_{!} gives a monoidal functor cl:𝒟+​(MHM⁡(ℳ𝒜))→𝒟+​(MHM⁡(K⁡(𝒜)))\mathrm{cl}\colon\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}))\rightarrow\mathcal{D}^{+}(\mathrm{MHM}(\K(\mathcal{A}))). We can then consider the compactly supported CoHA of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, defined as cl!𝒜¯𝒜\mathrm{cl}_{!}\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}. A subalgebra is given by the compactly supported BPS algebra cl!ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg\mathrm{cl}_{!}\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}, and we define cl!ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie\mathrm{cl}_{!}\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}} to be the compactly supported BPS Lie algebra. A corollary of Theorems 1.1 and 1.7 is the following.

Corollary 7.17.
  1. (1)

    The compactly supported BPS algebra cl!ℬ𝒫𝒮𝒜,Alg\mathrm{cl}_{!}\mathcal{BPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}} is isomorphic to 𝐔⁡(𝔫K⁡(𝒜),(−,−)𝒞,IPc+)\UEA(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}},\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{c}}}) where

    IPc:ΦK⁡(𝒜)+→𝐍[t±1/2]m↦IPc​(𝒢𝒜,m)=∑j∈𝐙dimHj(𝒢𝒜,m)t−j/2.\begin{matrix}\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{c}}&\colon&\Phi^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A})}&\rightarrow&\mathbf{N}[t^{\pm 1/2}]\\ &&m&\mapsto&\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathscr{G}_{\mathcal{A},m})&=\sum_{j\in\mathbf{Z}}\dim\HO^{j}(\mathscr{G}_{\mathcal{A},m})t^{-j/2}.\end{matrix}
  2. (2)

    We have a PBW isomorphism

    Sym(𝔫K⁡(𝒜),(−,−)𝒞,IPc+⊗H𝐂∗∗)→cl!𝒜𝒜.\Sym\left(\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)_{\mathscr{C}},\mathrm{IP}_{\mathrm{c}}}\otimes\HO^{*}_{\mathbf{C}^{*}}\right)\rightarrow\mathrm{cl}_{!}\mathscr{A}_{\mathcal{A}}.
Proof.

Both statements are straightforward consequences of Theorem 1.1, and the description of the weight function uses that 𝒢𝒜,m\mathscr{G}_{\mathcal{A},m} is Verdier self-dual and so Hc∗⁡(𝒢𝒜,m)≅H∗⁡(𝒢𝒜,m)∗\HO^{*}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathscr{G}_{\mathcal{A},m})\cong\HO^{*}(\mathscr{G}_{\mathcal{A},m})^{*} (the second star in the r.h.s. indicates the graded linear dual).

∎

7.9. Weyl-group invariance

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a 2-Calabi–Yau category as in Definition 7.15, and let 𝒢¯𝒜∈MHM⁡(ℳ𝒜)\underline{\mathscr{G}}_{\mathcal{A}}\in\mathrm{MHM}(\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}) be defined as above (see §6.4.3). Let ı△:ℳ𝒜△↪ℳ𝒜\imath_{\triangle}\colon\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\triangle}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} be the inclusion of monoids corresponding to a Serre subcategory, and let us assume that if ℳ𝒜,m⊆ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m}\subseteq\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} is a connected component corresponding to a real simple root mm, then ℳ𝒜,m△=ℳ𝒜,m\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m}^{\triangle}=\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A},m}. It follows that the weight function P:ΦM,(−,−)+→𝐍[t±1/2]P\colon\Phi_{M,(-,-)}^{+}\rightarrow\mathbf{N}[t^{\pm 1/2}] defining the generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebra 𝔤𝒜△\mathfrak{g}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}} satisfies P⁡(m)=1P(m)=1, as required by the definition of GKM algebras in §3.2.

We define the graph Γ\Gamma as follows: the vertices VV of Γ\Gamma are labelled by real simple roots a∈Φ𝒜+,a\in\Phi_{\mathcal{A}}^{+,\real} of 𝒜\mathcal{A}. If ii and jj are two vertices of Γ\Gamma, then we have −(i,j)𝒞-(i,j)_{\mathscr{C}} edges between them. Let WΓW_{\Gamma} be the Weyl group associated to the graph Γ\Gamma: it is the subgroup of the group of linear automorphisms of 𝐂V\mathbf{C}^{V} generated by the reflections

si​(λ)=λ−λT​Ci​1is_{i}(\lambda)=\lambda-\lambda^{T}C_{i}1_{i}

where CiC_{i} is the iith column of the Cartan matrix defined by Ci​j=2​δi​j−#⁡{edges between ​i​ and ​j}C_{ij}=2\delta_{ij}-\#\{\textrm{edges between }i\textrm{ and }j\}. Let M^\widehat{M} denote the groupification of K⁡(𝒜)\K(\mathcal{A}). The group WΓW_{\Gamma} acts similarly on M^⊗𝐙𝐂\widehat{M}\otimes_{\mathbf{Z}}\mathbf{C} by reflections:

si​(m)=m−(m,i)𝒞​i.s_{i}(m)=m-(m,i)_{\mathscr{C}}i.
Proposition 7.18.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a 2-Calabi–Yau category, and let ı△:ℳ𝒜△↪ℳ𝒜\imath_{\triangle}\colon\mathcal{M}^{\triangle}_{\mathcal{A}}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}} be as above. Let m,m′∈K⁡(𝒜)m,m^{\prime}\in\K(\mathcal{A}) satisfy w⁡(m)=m′w(m)=m^{\prime}, where w∈WΓw\in W_{\Gamma} and WΓW_{\Gamma} is the Weyl group defined above. Then there is an isomorphism of weight spaces

(7.3) 𝔫𝒜,mBPS,△,+≅𝔫𝒜,m′BPS,△,+.\mathfrak{n}_{\mathcal{A},m}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle,+}\cong\mathfrak{n}_{\mathcal{A},m^{\prime}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle,+}.
Proof.

Let 𝔤⊆𝔤𝒜BPS,△\mathfrak{g}\subseteq\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle} be the Kac–Moody Lie algebra generated by the subspace

⨁m∈ΦK⁡(𝒜),(−,−)+,(𝔤𝒜,mBPS,△+𝔤𝒜,−mBPS,△).\bigoplus_{m\in\Phi_{\K(\mathcal{A}),(-,-)}^{+,\real}}\left(\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{A},m}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle}+\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{A},-m}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle}\right).

In other words, we set 𝔤\mathfrak{g} to be the Kac–Moody Lie algebra associated to the (half) Ext quiver of the union of objects in 𝒜\mathcal{A} corresponding to real simple roots. Then 𝔤𝒜BPS,△\mathfrak{g}_{\mathcal{A}}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},\triangle} is an integrable 𝔤\mathfrak{g}-representation, and the claim follows by general theory of Kac–Moody Lie algebras [Kac90, Proposition 3.7a)]. ∎

8. Comparison with the 3D BPS Lie algebra and cohomological integrality for 2CY categories

8.1. BPS Lie algebras for Jacobi algebras

The BPS Lie algebra associated to a quiver with general potential, or Jacobi algebra, was defined in [DM20, §6.1, Corollary 6.11]. We briefly recall the definitions, and refer to [KS11, Dav17a, DM20] for background and full details. While the theory we present here, as in the rest of the paper, can readily be lifted to categories of (monodromic) mixed Hodge modules/mixed Hodge structures, we describe everything at the level of perverse sheaves/vector spaces.

Let QQ be a quiver, which we assume to be symmetric (i.e. for every pair of vertices i,j∈Q0i,j\in Q_{0} we assume that there are as many arrows from ii to jj as there are from jj to ii). We fix a bilinear form ψ:𝐙Q0×𝐙Q0→𝐙\psi\colon\mathbf{Z}^{Q_{0}}\times\mathbf{Z}^{Q_{0}}\rightarrow\mathbf{Z} satisfying the condition

ψ(𝐝′′,𝐝′)+ψ(𝐝′,𝐝′′)≡χQ(𝐝′,𝐝′)χQ(𝐝′′,𝐝′′)+χQ(𝐝′,𝐝′′)(mod2),\psi(\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime})+\psi(\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime})\equiv\chi_{Q}(\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime})\chi_{Q}(\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime})+\chi_{Q}(\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime})\quad\pmod{2},

as in [KS11, §2.6], or [DM20, §1.6]. We next pick a potential W∈𝐂​Q/[𝐂​Q,𝐂​Q]W\in\mathbf{C}Q/[\mathbf{C}Q,\mathbf{C}Q]. The potential WW defines a function Tr⁡(W)\Tr(W) on 𝔐Q,𝐝\mathfrak{M}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}, sending a 𝐂​Q\mathbf{C}Q-module ρ\rho to Tr(W¯⋅:ρ→ρ)\Tr(\overline{W}\cdot\colon\rho\rightarrow\rho) where W¯\overline{W} is any lift of WW to 𝐂​Q\mathbf{C}Q. This function factors through 𝙹𝙷:𝔐Q,𝐝→ℳQ,𝐝\JH\colon\mathfrak{M}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}. We define

𝒜Q,W,𝐝≔𝙹𝙷∗⁡ϕTr⁡(W)𝔭​𝐐𝔐Q,𝐝vir\mathscr{A}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}}\coloneqq\JH_{*}{}^{\mathfrak{p}}\!\phi_{\Tr(W)}\mathbf{Q}^{\mathrm{vir}}_{\mathfrak{M}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}}

where 𝐐𝔐Q,𝐝vir≔𝐐𝔐Q,𝐝​[−χQ​(𝐝,𝐝)]\mathbf{Q}_{\mathfrak{M}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}}^{\mathrm{vir}}\coloneqq\mathbf{Q}_{\mathfrak{M}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}}[-\chi_{Q}(\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d})], and 𝒜Q,W≔⨁𝐝∈𝐍Q0𝒜Q,W,𝐝\mathscr{A}_{Q,W}\coloneqq\bigoplus_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}}\mathscr{A}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}}, with ϕTr⁡(W)𝔭{}^{\mathfrak{p}}\!\phi_{\Tr(W)} the perverse vanishing cycles functor for the function Tr⁡(W)\Tr(W). Via pushforward and pullback in vanishing cycle cohomology, along morphisms from the stack of short exact sequences of 𝐂​Q\mathbf{C}Q-modules, along with the Thom–Sebastiani isomorphism, the complex 𝒜Q,W\mathscr{A}_{Q,W} carries the structure of an algebra object in 𝒟+​(Perv⁡(ℳQ))≅𝒟c+​(ℳQ)\mathcal{D}^{+}(\operatorname{Perv}(\mathcal{M}_{Q}))\cong\mathcal{D}^{+}_{\mathrm{c}}(\mathcal{M}_{Q}), [KS11, Dav17a]. The monoidal structure on this category is defined via the direct image along the direct sum map ⊕:ℳQ×ℳQ→ℳQ\oplus\colon\mathcal{M}_{Q}\times\mathcal{M}_{Q}\rightarrow\mathcal{M}_{Q}. As usual, we denote by 𝒜Q,Wψ\mathscr{A}_{Q,W}^{\psi} the ψ\psi-twisted CoHA, in which we twist the multiplication morphism 𝒜Q,W,𝐝′⊡𝒜Q,W,𝐝′′→𝒜Q,W,𝐝′+𝐝′′\mathscr{A}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}^{\prime}}\boxdot\mathscr{A}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime}}\rightarrow\mathscr{A}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}^{\prime}+\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime}} by (−1)ψ⁡(𝐝′,𝐝′′)(-1)^{\psi(\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime})}.

For 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} we define

ℬ​𝒫​𝒮Q,W,𝐝≔(τ⩽1𝔭​𝙹𝙷∗​ϕTr⁡(W)𝔭​𝐐𝔐Q,𝐝vir)​[1].\mathcal{BPS}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}}\coloneqq({{}^{\mathfrak{p}}\tau}^{\leqslant 1}\!\JH_{*}{}^{\mathfrak{p}}\!\phi_{\Tr(W)}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathfrak{M}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}}^{\mathrm{vir}})[1].

The following theorem is the basis for the definition of the BPS Lie algebra associated to a quiver with potential [DM20, Theorem C].

Theorem 8.1 ([DM20, Theorem C, Corollary 6.11]).

The complex ℬ​𝒫​𝒮Q,W,𝐝\mathcal{BPS}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}} is a perverse sheaf. Setting 𝔤Q,W,𝐝≔H∗⁡ℬ​𝒫​𝒮Q,W,𝐝​[−1]\mathfrak{g}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}}\coloneqq\HO^{*}\!\mathcal{BPS}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}}[-1] and 𝔤Q,W≔⨁𝐝∈𝐍Q0𝔤Q,W,𝐝\mathfrak{g}_{Q,W}\coloneqq\bigoplus_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}}\mathfrak{g}_{Q,W,\mathbf{d}}, the natural morphism 𝔤Q,W→H∗⁡𝒜Q,W\mathfrak{g}_{Q,W}\rightarrow\HO^{*}\!\mathscr{A}_{Q,W} is an injection, and the image is closed under the commutator Lie bracket for the algebra H∗⁡𝒜Q,Wψ\HO^{*}\!\mathscr{A}_{Q,W}^{\psi}.

The resulting 𝐍Q0\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}-graded Lie algebra is denoted 𝔤Q,Wψ\mathfrak{g}_{Q,W}^{\psi}. We include the superscript ψ\psi since a priori this algebra depends on the bilinear form ψ\psi (in contrast with the Lie algebra 𝔫𝒜+\mathfrak{n}_{\mathcal{A}}^{+} we have associated with a 2CY category 𝒜\mathcal{A}). We use the notation 𝔤Q,W\mathfrak{g}_{Q,W} as opposed to 𝔫Q,W+\mathfrak{n}^{+}_{Q,W}, following [DM20]. In the case of the tripled quiver with potential §8.2, the Lie algebra 𝔤Q,Wψ\mathfrak{g}_{Q,W}^{\psi} appears a posteriori to be a half of a GKM Lie algebra (by Proposition 8.4 and our main result Theorem 1.2), and so one could have expected the letter 𝔫\mathfrak{n}.

8.2. Tripled quiver with potential

Let QQ be a quiver, and denote by Q~\widetilde{Q} the tripled quiver of QQ defined in §2. We denote by

so in particular we may retain our assumed choice of ψ\psi: we set ψ⁡(𝐝′,𝐝′′)=χQ​(𝐝′,𝐝′′)\psi(\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime})=\chi_{Q}(\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d}^{\prime\prime}). Theorem 8.2 ([Dav20, Theorem 4.1 and 6.1] ).

The complex ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie𝟹​𝚍≔h∗​ℬ​𝒫​𝒮Q~,W~​[−1]=h∗​τ⩽1𝔭​𝙹𝙷∗​ϕTr⁡(W)𝔭​𝐐𝔐Qvir\mathcal{BPS}^{\mathtt{3d}}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}\coloneqq h_{*}\mathcal{BPS}_{\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{W}}[-1]=h_{*}{{}^{\mathfrak{p}}\tau}^{\leqslant 1}\!\JH_{*}{}^{\mathfrak{p}}\!\phi_{\Tr(W)}\mathbf{Q}_{\mathfrak{M}_{Q}}^{\mathrm{vir}} is a perverse sheaf. Moreover, the morphism

is an isomorphism of algebra objects. There is a natural isomorphism of Lie algebras H∗⁡ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie𝟹​𝚍,ψ≅𝔤Q~,W~ψ\HO^{*}\!\mathcal{BPS}^{\mathtt{3d},\psi}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}\cong\mathfrak{g}_{\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{W}}^{\psi}.

obtained by evaluating symmetric tensors with the aid of the algebra structure on the target.

The map PBWΠQ\mathrm{PBW}_{\Pi_{Q}} is an isomorphism of perverse sheaves.

Proposition 8.4.

There is a natural morphism

ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie→ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie𝟹​𝚍,ψ\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}\rightarrow\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}^{\mathtt{3d},\psi}

in Perv⁡(ℳΠQ)\operatorname{Perv}(\mathcal{M}_{\Pi_{Q}}). It is an isomorphism of Lie algebra objects. Taking derived global sections, there is an isomorphism of Lie algebras

𝔫ΠQBPS,+≅𝔤Q~,W~ψ.\mathfrak{n}^{\mathtt{\aBPS},+}_{\Pi_{Q}}\cong\mathfrak{g}_{\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{W}}^{\psi}.
Proof.

By Theorem 1.1 there is a monomorphism of Lie algebra objects

(8.2) ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie→ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Algψ\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}\rightarrow\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}

and by [Dav20, Formula 67] there is a monomorphism

(8.3) ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie𝟹​𝚍,ψ→ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Algψ.\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}^{\mathtt{3d},\psi}\rightarrow\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}.

In both instances we consider the target as a Lie algebra object via the commutator bracket. By Theorem 1.1 again, ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}} can be written as a quotient of Free⊡-Lie⁡(𝒢ΠQ)\operatorname{Free}_{\boxdot\sLie}(\mathscr{G}_{\Pi_{Q}}), and in particular for each 𝐝∈ΦΠQ+\mathbf{d}\in\Phi^{+}_{\Pi_{Q}} the semisimple perverse sheaf ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}} contains a unique copy of 𝒢𝐝\mathscr{G}_{\mathbf{d}}. Since ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie𝟹​𝚍\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}^{\mathtt{3d}} contains 𝒢𝐝\mathscr{G}_{\mathbf{d}} for each 𝐝∈ΦΠQ+\mathbf{d}\in\Phi^{+}_{\Pi_{Q}} [Dav20, §7], the morphism (8.2) factors uniquely through (8.3). We therefore have monomorphisms of Lie algebra objects.

(8.4) ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie→ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie𝟹​𝚍,ψ→ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Algψ.\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}\rightarrow\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}^{\mathtt{3d},\psi}\rightarrow\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}.

By evaluating symmetric products using the algebra structure on ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Algψ\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi}, we obtain from (8.4) the morphisms of perverse sheaves

The composition Sym⊡⁡(ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Lie)→ℬ​𝒫​𝒮ΠQ,Algψ\Sym_{\boxdot}(\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}})\rightarrow\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi} is an isomorphism by Theorem 1.1 and the second arrow in (8.5) is the morphism PBWΠQ\mathrm{PBW}_{\Pi_{Q}}, which is an isomorphism by Proposition 8.3. Therefore the first arrow in (8.5) is an isomorphism, and consequently the first arrow in (8.4) is also an isomorphism. ∎

Let QQ be a quiver, and let Γ\Gamma be the underlying graph of QQ. The Weyl group WΓW_{\Gamma} acts on 𝐂Q0\mathbf{C}^{Q_{0}}, and its image is generated by the reflections

with ii a vertex that supports no 1-cycles, i.e. i∈Q0i\in Q_{0} (see also §7.9).

Corollary 8.5.

Let QQ be a quiver, and let 𝐝,𝐝′∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d}^{\prime}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} be dimension vectors such that w⋅𝐝=𝐝′w\cdot\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{d}^{\prime} for some w∈WΓw\in W_{\Gamma}. Then there is an isomorphism

𝔤Q~,W~,𝐝≅𝔤Q~,W~,𝐝′.\mathfrak{g}_{\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{W},\mathbf{d}}\cong\mathfrak{g}_{\widetilde{Q},\widetilde{W},\mathbf{d}^{\prime}}.

This follows from combining Propositions 7.18 and 8.4. ∎

Using the characterisation (9.4) of Kac polynomials in terms of characteristic functions of BPS cohomology, we obtain a new proof of the Weyl-invariance of Kac polynomials

AQ,𝐝​(q)=AQ,w⋅𝐝​(q)A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)=A_{Q,w\cdot\mathbf{d}}(q)

which is part of Theorem 1 of Kac’s original paper [Kac83].

8.3. Cohomological integrality and PBW isomorphism for 22-Calabi–Yau categories

8.3.1. Restriction of BPS Lie algebras

We let ℱ¯={ℱ1,…,ℱr}\underline{\mathcal{F}}=\{\mathcal{F}_{1},\ldots,\mathcal{F}_{r}\} be a Σ\Sigma-collection in an Abelian category 𝒜\mathcal{A}, satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 4.2, where 𝒜\mathcal{A} also satisfies Assumptions 1–6 from §4.3 and §4.4, so that we can define the BPS Lie algebra for 𝒜\mathcal{A}. We let QQ be a half Ext-quiver of the collection ℱ¯\underline{\mathcal{F}}.

Lemma 8.6.

Let ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯ΠQ,Lie\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}} be the BPS Lie algebra sheaf on ℳΠQ\mathcal{M}_{\Pi_{Q}} and let ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}} be the BPS Lie algebra sheaf on ℳ𝒜\mathcal{M}_{\mathcal{A}}. Then with the notations of diagram (7.1), we have a canonical isomorphism of Lie algebras ı𝒩!ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯ΠQ,Lie≅ıℱ¯!ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie\imath_{\mathcal{N}}^{!}\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}\cong\imath_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}^{!}\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}.

Proof.

Once again, we may prove this lemma after applying the functor 𝐫𝐚𝐭\rat. Then it follows from Lemma 7.1, Proposition 5.3 and Lemma 7.3. More precisely, ı𝒩!ℬ𝒫𝒮ΠQ,Lieψ\imath_{\mathcal{N}}^{!}\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Lie}}^{\psi} is the sub-Lie algebra of ι𝒩!ℬ𝒫𝒮ΠQ,Algψ\iota_{\mathcal{N}}^{!}\mathcal{BPS}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi} generated by ι𝒩!𝒢ΠQ,𝐝\iota_{\mathcal{N}}^{!}\mathscr{G}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathbf{d}} for 𝐝∈ΦΠQ+\mathbf{d}\in\Phi^{+}_{\Pi_{Q}} and ıℱ¯!ℬ𝒫𝒮𝒜,Lieψ\imath_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}^{!}\mathcal{BPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}^{\psi} is the sub-Lie algebra of ıℱ¯!ℬ𝒫𝒮𝒜,Algψ\imath_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}^{!}\mathcal{BPS}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi} generated by ι!ℱ¯𝒢𝒜,m\iota^{!}_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}\mathscr{G}_{\mathcal{A},m}, m∈Φ𝒜+m\in\Phi^{+}_{\mathcal{A}}, and for 𝐝∈ΦΠQ+\mathbf{d}\in\Phi^{+}_{\Pi_{Q}}, ι𝒩,𝐝!𝒢ΠQ,𝐝≅ιℱ¯,λℱ¯​(𝐝)!𝒢𝒜,λℱ¯​(𝐝)\iota_{\mathcal{N},\mathbf{d}}^{!}\mathscr{G}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathbf{d}}\cong\iota_{\underline{\mathcal{F}},\lambda_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}(\mathbf{d})}^{!}\mathscr{G}_{\mathcal{A},\lambda_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}}(\mathbf{d})} as in the proof of Proposition 7.4 (where λℱ¯\lambda_{\underline{\mathcal{F}}} is defined in §4.6.1), which moreover satisfy the same Serre relations (using Lemma 5.2). ∎

8.3.2. Proof of the cohomological integrality theorem for 2CY categories

We prove Theorem 1.7. We first construct the morphism Ψ𝒜\Psi_{\mathcal{A}}.

Composing the adjunction morphism ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Alg=τ⩽0​𝒜¯𝒜→𝒜¯𝒜\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}=\tau^{\leqslant 0}\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}} with the inclusion ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie→ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Algψ\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Alg}}^{\psi} provided by Theorem 1.1, we have a canonical morphism

ℬ​𝒫​𝒮¯𝒜,Lie→𝒜¯𝒜.\underline{\mathcal{BPS}}_{\mathcal{A},\mathrm{Lie}}\rightarrow\underline{\mathscr{A}}_{\mathcal{A}}.

We fix a positive determinant line bundle on 𝔐𝒜\mathfrak{M}_{\mathcal{A}}. 9. Cuspidal polynomials of quivers

9.1. Cuspidal polynomials

Our main theorem (Theorem 1.2) can be applied to proving the positivity of absolutely cuspidal polynomials of quivers [BS19], a strengthening of the Kac positivity conjecture [Kac83, Conjecture 2], in full generality.

Let Q=(Q1,Q0,s,t:Q1→Q0)Q=(Q_{1},Q_{0},s,t\colon Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0}) be a quiver. In the early ’90s Ringel and Green defined [Rin90, Rin92, Gre95] the Hall bialgebra of QQ over a finite field 𝐅q\mathbf{F}_{q}. As a vector space over 𝐂\mathbf{C}, it has a basis given by the set of isomorphism classes of representations of QQ over 𝐅q\mathbf{F}_{q}:

HQ,𝐅q:=⨁[M]∈RepQ(𝐅q)/∼𝐂[M]H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}:=\bigoplus_{[M]\in\operatorname{Rep}_{Q}(\mathbf{F}_{q})/\sim}\mathbf{C}[M]

where RepQ⁡(𝐅q)\operatorname{Rep}_{Q}(\mathbf{F}_{q}) denotes the category of finite-dimensional modules and the product is the usual Hall-type product: we recommend [Sch06] for background. Green [Gre95] defined a coproduct Δ\Delta on HQ,𝐅qH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}, so that HQ,𝐅qH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}} has the structure of a twisted Hopf algebra (see Xiao’s paper [Xia97] for an explicit description of the antipode). The twist, which won’t be used in this paper, is explained in [loc. cit.].

Sevenhant and Van den Bergh proved [SV01] that HQ,𝐅qH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}} has the structure of the positive part of the quantised enveloping algebra of a generalised Kac–Moody algebra with deformation parameter specialised at q\sqrt{q}. The generators are given by the space of cuspidal functions. These are by definition the primitive elements of the coproduct:

HQ,𝐅qcusp={f∈HQ,𝐅q∣Δ⁡(f)=f⊗1+1⊗f},H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{cusp}}=\{f\in H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}\mid\Delta(f)=f\otimes 1+1\otimes f\},

satisfying Serre relations, see [Hen21, Theorem 3.4] for a detailed formulation. In [SV01] it is assumed that the quiver is loop-free, although this assumption can be removed.

For 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}, let MQ,𝐝​(q)M_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q) be the number of isomorphism classes of 𝐅q\mathbf{F}_{q}–representations of QQ of dimension vector 𝐝\mathbf{d}, and let IQ,𝐝​(q)I_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q) be the number of isomorphism classes of indecomposable 𝐅q\mathbf{F}_{q}–representations of QQ of dimension vector 𝐝\mathbf{d}. We denote by AQ,𝐝​(q)A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q) the Kac polynomial, counting the number of isomorphism classes of absolutely indecomposable 𝐅q\mathbf{F}_{q}–representations of QQ of dimension vector 𝐝\mathbf{d}. By Kac [Kac83], all of these functions are polynomials in qq. Moreover, by [HLR13] (or [Dav18, DGT16] for different approaches), the coefficients of AQ,𝐝​(q)A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q) are nonnegative, as originally conjectured by Kac in [Kac83].

Given a 𝐍Q0\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}-graded vector space VV, we define ch⁡(V)=∑𝐝∈𝐍Q0dim(V𝐝)​z𝐝\mathrm{ch}(V)=\sum_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}}\dim(V_{\mathbf{d}})z^{\mathbf{d}}. If VV also carries a cohomological 𝐙\mathbf{Z}-grading, we define

ch𝐙​(V)≔∑n∈𝐙∑𝐝∈𝐙Q0dim(V𝐝n)​qn/2​z𝐝.\mathrm{ch}^{\mathbf{Z}}(V)\coloneqq\sum_{n\in\mathbf{Z}}\sum_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{Z}^{Q_{0}}}\dim(V_{\mathbf{d}}^{n})q^{n/2}z^{\mathbf{d}}.

The 𝐍Q0\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}-graded character of the Hall algebra is given by the formula

(9.1) ch⁡(HQ,Fq)=∑𝐝∈𝐍Q0MQ,𝐝​(q)​z𝐝=Expz⁡(∑𝐝>0IQ,𝐝​(q)​z𝐝)=Expq,z⁡(∑𝐝>0AQ,𝐝​(q)​z𝐝),\mathrm{ch}(H_{Q,F_{q}})=\sum_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}}M_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)z^{\mathbf{d}}=\Exp_{z}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{d}>0}I_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)z^{\mathbf{d}}\right)=\Exp_{q,z}\left(\sum_{\mathbf{d}>0}A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)z^{\mathbf{d}}\right),

where Expz\Exp_{z} and Expq,z\Exp_{q,z} denote the plethystic exponentials, see [BS19, §1.5]. The second equality follows from the Krull–Schmidt property of the category of representations of the quiver and the third from Galois descent for quiver representations.

The space HQ,𝐅qcuspH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{cusp}} is naturally graded by the dimension vector: HQ,𝐅qcusp=⨁𝐝∈𝐍Q0HQ,𝐅qcusp​[𝐝]H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{cusp}}=\bigoplus_{\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}}H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{cusp}}[\mathbf{d}]. There has been a growing interest in understanding this space and to find a parametrisation of cuspidal functions [BS19, Hen21]. The first step was to compute its dimension. We have the following result.

Theorem 9.1 ([BS19, Theorem 1.1]).

The dimension dim𝐂HQ,𝐅qcusp​[𝐝]\dim_{\mathbf{C}}H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{cusp}}[\mathbf{d}] is given by a polynomial with rational coefficients CQ,𝐝​(q)∈𝐐​[q]C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)\in\mathbf{Q}[q].

The vector space HQ,𝐅qcusp​[𝐝]H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{cusp}}[\mathbf{d}] is ungraded, and its dimension is determined by qq, via the evaluation of the polynomial CQ,𝐝​(q)C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q). We will see that this same polynomial is obtained as the characteristic function of a fixed cohomologically graded vector space.

see [BS19].

9.2. Intersection Poincaré polynomials of singular quiver varieties

The canonical decomposition of a dimension vector 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} is the unique decomposition of 𝐝\mathbf{d} as a sum of primitive positive roots (elements of ΣΠQ\Sigma_{\Pi_{Q}}) such that any other decomposition as a sum of primitive positive roots is a refinement of it. By [Cra02], it is well-defined and unique. Moreover, it gives a product decomposition of the corresponding quiver variety [Cra02].

Corollary 9.7.

Let 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} be a dimension vector and 𝐝=∑j=1rmj​𝐝j\mathbf{d}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}m_{j}\mathbf{d}_{j} be the canonical decomposition of 𝐝\mathbf{d}, where the 𝐝j\mathbf{d}_{j} are pairwise distinct, 𝐝j∈ΣΠQ\mathbf{d}_{j}\in\Sigma_{\Pi_{Q}} and mj⩾0m_{j}\geqslant 0. We have

IP⁡(ℳΠQ,𝐝)​(t)=∏j=1r1mj!​((dd​u)mj​Expt,u⁡(CQ,𝐝jabs​(t−2)​u))u=0\mathrm{IP}(\mathcal{M}_{\Pi_{Q},\mathbf{d}})(t)=\prod_{j=1}^{r}\frac{1}{m_{j}!}\left(\left(\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}u}\right)^{m_{j}}\Exp_{t,u}(C_{Q,\mathbf{d}_{j}}^{\mathrm{abs}}(t^{-2})u)\right)_{u=0}

where uu is an additional formal variable and Expt,u\Exp_{t,u} the plethystic exponential.

Proof.

This follows from the product decomposition of quiver varieties [Cra02, Theorem 1.1] and the formula for intersection Poincaré polynomials of symmetric products. ∎

The canonical decomposition of a dimension vector 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} can be determined algorithmically. Indeed, for a given 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}}, it is possible to determine the set of primitive positive roots 𝐝′⩽𝐝\mathbf{d}^{\prime}\leqslant\mathbf{d} (this amounts to checking a certain finite number of inequalities for all decompositions of 𝐝′\mathbf{d}^{\prime}). Then, Crawley-Boevey proves that the canonical decomposition is such that any other decomposition of 𝐝\mathbf{d} as a sum of elements of ΣΠQ\Sigma_{\Pi_{Q}} refines it. Therefore, we can start from the trivial decomposition 𝐝=∑j=1r𝐝j≔∑i∈Q0di​1i\mathbf{d}=\sum_{j=1}^{r}\mathbf{d}_{j}\coloneqq\sum_{i\in Q_{0}}d_{i}1_{i} where each 𝐝j\mathbf{d}_{j} is equal to 1i1_{i} for some vertex i∈Q0i\in Q_{0}. We can then iteratively combine some of the dimension vectors 𝐝j\mathbf{d}_{j} when their sum is in ΣΠQ\Sigma_{\Pi_{Q}}. In conclusion, intersection Poincaré polynomials of all quiver varieties can be algorithmically computed using our results.

9.3. (Semi)-nilpotent Kac and cuspidal polynomials

Bozec, Schiffmann and Vasserot defined in [BSV20] various families of counting polynomials for quiver representations over finite fields, obtained by imposing appropriate nilpotency conditions. They related the polynomials obtained this way to the count of points of some quiver varieties. In this section, we recall these definitions and we define the corresponding cuspidal and absolutely cuspidal polynomials, following [BS19]. We use the general results from this paper to prove the positivity for these polynomials.

9.3.1. Nilpotent and semi-nilpotent representations of quivers

We recall various notions of nilpotency for quiver representations from [BSV20]. Let Q=(Q0,Q1)Q=(Q_{0},Q_{1}) be a quiver. A representation MM of QQ is called

  1. (1)

    nilpotent if there exists a flag of Q0Q_{0}-graded vector spaces {0}=M0⊆M1⊆…⊆Mr=M\{0\}=M_{0}\subseteq M_{1}\subseteq\ldots\subseteq M_{r}=M such that the action of arrows of QQ sends MiM_{i} to Mi−1M_{i-1};

  2. (2)

    11-nilpotent if there exists a flag of Q0Q_{0}-graded vector spaces {0}=M0⊆M1⊆…⊆Mr=M\{0\}=M_{0}\subseteq M_{1}\subseteq\ldots\subseteq M_{r}=M such that loops of QQ send MiM_{i} to Mi−1M_{i-1} (no conditions for other arrows).

Let Q¯=(Q0,Q¯1)\overline{Q}=(Q_{0},\overline{Q}_{1}) be the double of the quiver QQ. We have Q¯1=Q1⊔Q1∗\overline{Q}_{1}=Q_{1}\sqcup Q_{1}^{*}, and each arrow α∈Q1\alpha\in Q_{1} has an opposite arrow α∗∈Q1∗\alpha^{*}\in Q_{1}^{*}. A representation MM of Q¯\overline{Q} is called

  1. (1)

    semi-nilpotent if there exists a flag of Q0Q_{0}-graded vector spaces {0}=M0⊆M1⊆…⊆Mr=M\{0\}=M_{0}\subseteq M_{1}\subseteq\ldots\subseteq M_{r}=M such that arrows α∈Q1\alpha\in Q_{1} send MiM_{i} to Mi−1M_{i-1} and arrows α∈Q1∗\alpha\in Q_{1}^{*} send MiM_{i} to MiM_{i}.

  2. (2)

    strictly semi-nilpotent if there exists a flag of Q0Q_{0}-graded vector spaces {0}=M0⊆M1⊆…⊆Mr=M\{0\}=M_{0}\subseteq M_{1}\subseteq\ldots\subseteq M_{r}=M such that consecutive subquotients are supported at a single vertex, each arrow α∈Q1\alpha\in Q_{1} sends MiM_{i} to Mi−1M_{i-1} and arrows α∈Q1∗\alpha\in Q_{1}^{*} send MiM_{i} to MiM_{i}.

  3. (3)

    ∗*-semi-nilpotent if the condition semi-nilpotent (1) is satisfied with Q1Q_{1} and Q1∗Q_{1}^{*} exchanged.

  4. (4)

    ∗*-strictly semi-nilpotent if the condition strictly semi-nilpotent (2) with Q1Q_{1} and Q1∗Q_{1}^{*} exchanged is satisfied.

Since the involution of ΠQ\Pi_{Q} swapping each arrow aa with a∗a^{*} swaps (3) with (1) and (4) with (2), the BPS cohomology for the ∗*-versions is isomorphic to the non-∗*-versions, which we concentrate on exclusively from now on.

9.3.2. Hall algebras

Recall from §9.1 that we have the Hall algebra of QQ over a finite field 𝐅q\mathbf{F}_{q}, HQ,𝐅qH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}, which is a bialgebra. We define similarly

HQ,𝐅qnil≔⨁[M]∈RepQ(𝐅q))/∼M​ is nilpotent𝐂⁡[M];HQ,𝐅q1​-nil≔⨁[M]∈RepQ(𝐅q))/∼M​ is 1-nilpotent𝐂⁡[M].H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{nil}}\coloneqq\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}[M]\in\operatorname{Rep}_{Q}(\mathbf{F}_{q}))/\sim\\ M\text{ is nilpotent}\end{subarray}}\mathbf{C}[M];\quad\quad H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{1\snil}\coloneqq\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}[M]\in\operatorname{Rep}_{Q}(\mathbf{F}_{q}))/\sim\\ M\text{ is $1$-nilpotent}\end{subarray}}\mathbf{C}[M].

Since the categories RepQnil⁡(𝐅q)\operatorname{Rep}_{Q}^{\mathrm{nil}}(\mathbf{F}_{q}) and RepQ1​-nil⁡(𝐅q)\operatorname{Rep}_{Q}^{1\snil}(\mathbf{F}_{q}) of nilpotent and 11-nilpotent representations of QQ are Serre subcategories (i.e. stable under extension, subobjects and quotients), HQ,𝐅nil⊆HQ,𝐅q1​-nil⊆HQ,𝐅qH_{Q,\mathbf{F}}^{\mathrm{nil}}\subseteq H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{1\snil}\subseteq H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}} are inclusions of biagebras.

9.3.3. Kac polynomials

In [BSV20] Bozec, Schiffmann and Vasserot defined and studied Kac polynomials for the categories RepQnil⁡(𝐅q)\operatorname{Rep}_{Q}^{\mathrm{nil}}(\mathbf{F}_{q}) and RepQ1​-nil⁡(𝐅q)\operatorname{Rep}_{Q}^{1\snil}(\mathbf{F}_{q}) (in particular by relating them to point counts of Nakajima quiver varieties). Namely, one may define as in §9.1 the counting functions MQ,𝐝nil​(q)M_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{nil}}(q), IQ,𝐝nil​(q)I_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{nil}}(q) and AQ,𝐝nil​(q)A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{nil}}(q), MQ,𝐝1​-nil​(q)M_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{1\snil}(q), IQ,𝐝1​-nil​(q)I_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{1\snil}(q) and AQ,𝐝1​-nil​(q)A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{1\snil}(q) for any 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} by considering respectively nilpotent and 11-nilpotent representations of QQ, and all, or indecomposable, or absolutely indecomposable isomorphism classes of such representations.

In both the cases of nilpotent and of 11-nilpotent representations, we have the sequence of equalities analogous to (9.1) and by [BSV20], all these counting functions are polynomials in qq. The analogue of the Kac positivity conjecture was proved in [Dav20]:

Proposition 9.8 ([Dav20, §4.2]).

The nilpotent versions of Kac polynomials AQ,𝐝nil​(q)A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{nil}}(q) and AQ,𝐝1​-nil​(q)A_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{1\snil}(q) have nonnegative coefficients.

9.3.4. Cuspidal polynomials

We define cuspidal functions in HQ,𝐅qnilH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{nil}} and HQ,𝐅q1​-nilH_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{1\snil} as

HQ,𝐅qnil,cusp=HQ,𝐅qnil∩HQ,𝐅qcusp,HQ,𝐅q1​-nil,cusp=HQ,𝐅q1​-nil∩HQ,𝐅qcusp.H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{nil},\mathrm{cusp}}=H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{nil}}\cap H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{cusp}},\quad H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{1\snil,\mathrm{cusp}}=H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{1\snil}\cap H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{cusp}}.

We define the functions CQ,𝐝nil​(q)C^{\mathrm{nil}}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q) and CQ,𝐝1​-nil​(q)C^{1\snil}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q), 𝐝∈𝐍Q0\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{N}^{Q_{0}} as

CQ,𝐝nil​(q)≔dim𝐂HQ,𝐅qnil,cusp,CQ,𝐝1​-nil​(q)≔dim𝐂HQ,𝐅q1​-nil,cusp.C^{\mathrm{nil}}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)\coloneqq\dim_{\mathbf{C}}H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{\mathrm{nil},\mathrm{cusp}},\quad C^{1\snil}_{Q,\mathbf{d}}(q)\coloneqq\dim_{\mathbf{C}}H_{Q,\mathbf{F}_{q}}^{1\snil,\mathrm{cusp}}.

The inductive description of cuspidal functions CQ,𝐝C_{Q,\mathbf{d}} in [BS19] works without modification for nilpotent and 11-nilpotent representations and this together with the polynomiality result for the numbers of isoclasses of nilpotent and 11-nilpotent representations provides the polynomiality of the nilpotent versions of the functions CQ,𝐝nilC_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\mathrm{nil}} and CQ,𝐝1​-nilC_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{1\snil}. One of the key points is the validity of the Sevenhant–Van den Bergh theorem [SV01, Theorem 1.1] describing the Hall algebra of a quiver as a quantum group for quivers with loops and the categories of representations with or without nilpotency conditions. Sevenhant and Van den Bergh assume that the quiver under consideration is loop-free and do not consider the case of nilpotent representations, but their methods adapt in a straightforward way.

We define absolutely cuspidal polynomials by the same combinatorial procedure as in [BS19]. That is, for □∈{nil,1​-nil}\square\in\{\mathrm{nil},1\snil\}, we define CQ,𝐝□,abs​(q)C_{Q,\mathbf{d}}^{\square,\mathrm{abs}}(q) as

10. Nakajima quiver varieties and lowest weight modules

10.1. Semistable modules

Let Q=(Q1,Q0,s,t:Q1→Q0)Q=(Q_{1},Q_{0},s,t\colon Q_{1}\rightarrow Q_{0}) be a quiver. A (King) stability condition for QQ is a tuple ζ∈𝐐Q0\zeta\in\mathbf{Q}^{Q_{0}}. For 𝐝∈𝐙Q0∖{0}\mathbf{d}\in\mathbf{Z}^{Q_{0}}\smallsetminus\{0\} we define the slope

μζ(𝐝)=ζ⋅𝐝/|𝐝|\mu_{\zeta}(\mathbf{d})=\zeta\!\cdot\!\mathbf{d}/\lvert\mathbf{d}\lvert

and for ρ\rho a nonzero 𝐂​Q\mathbf{C}Q-module, we define μζ​(ρ)=μζ​(dimQ0(ρ))\mu_{\zeta}(\rho)=\mu_{\zeta}(\dim_{Q_{0}}(\rho)). Then ρ\rho is called ζ\zeta-semistable if for all nonzero proper submodules ρ′⊆ρ\rho^{\prime}\subseteq\rho we have μζ​(ρ′)⩽μζ​(ρ)\mu_{\zeta}(\rho^{\prime})\leqslant\mu_{\zeta}(\rho), and is called ζ\zeta-stable if the inequality is strict. A semistable module is called polystable if it is a direct sum of stable modules.

Fix a quiver QQ, a potential W∈𝐂​Q/[𝐂​Q,𝐂​Q]W\in\mathbf{C}Q/[\mathbf{C}Q,\mathbf{C}Q], a stability condition ζ∈𝐐Q0\zeta\in\mathbf{Q}^{Q_{0}}, and a slope θ∈𝐐\theta\in\mathbf{Q} such that for all dimension vectors 𝐝,𝐝′\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d}^{\prime} of ζ\zeta-slope θ\theta we have χQ​(𝐝,𝐝′)=χQ​(𝐝′,𝐝)\chi_{Q}(\mathbf{d},\mathbf{d}^{\prime})=\chi_{Q}(\mathbf{d}^{\prime},\mathbf{d}). This condition is called genericity, and will be automatic for all the quivers that we encounter, since they will be symmetric.

We denote by 𝔐Q,𝐝ζ​sst\mathfrak{M}^{\zeta\sstab}_{Q,\mathbf{d}} the moduli stack of 𝐝\mathbf{d}-dimensional ζ\zeta-semistable 𝐂​Q\mathbf{C}Q-modules, and by ℳQ,𝐝ζ​sst\mathcal{M}^{\zeta\sstab}_{Q,\mathbf{d}} the moduli scheme, constructed via GIT in [Kin94]. Points of ℳQ,𝐝ζ​sst\mathcal{M}^{\zeta\sstab}_{Q,\mathbf{d}} are in bijection with isomorphism classes of 𝐝\mathbf{d}-dimensional polystable 𝐂​Q\mathbf{C}Q-modules. Recall from §3.3 the definition of lowest weight modules over generalised Kac–Moody Lie algebras. We will use the following easy algebraic lemma.

10.4. Actions on cohomology of quiver varieties, revisited

10.4.1. Hilbert schemes of 𝐀2\mathbf{A}^{2} and Heisenberg algebras

First we recover the famous description of the cohomology of Hilbert schemes of 𝐀2\mathbf{A}^{2} as an irreducible lowest weight module for an infinite-dimensional Heisenberg algebra, as in [Nak99, Nak97].

Let QQ be the Jordan quiver, with one vertex and one loop, and let 𝐟=1\mathbf{f}=1, so that Q𝐟¯\overline{Q_{\mathbf{f}}} is the ADHM quiver (with the help of which the construction of instantons in [Ati+94] can be formulated):

It is easy to check that in this case (0,1)(0,1) is the only element of ΦΠQ𝐟+\Phi^{+}_{\Pi_{Q_{\mathbf{f}}}} of the form (n,1)(n,1) (using the characterisation given in Proposition 5.3 and the definition of the set of roots). In addition, there is a natural isomorphism [Nak99]
